articles.title: A Florida county discovered 14 Flock cameras nobody authorized, and 11 remain unclaimed
articles.text:
What we know so far: Flock's AI-powered surveillance cameras have already drawn widespread controversy even when authorities fully disclose their deployment. Communities across the US are canceling contracts with the company due to concerns over privacy and police abuse. However, in some areas, officials have found more cameras than were authorized and don't always know who is watching through them.
The latest case of unclaimed Flock cameras occurred in St. Lucie County, Florida. When officials began taking down the cameras after canceling the county's contract with the company, they discovered 14 extra cameras that the police say were not theirs.
The St. Lucie County's contract with Flock authorized 52 cameras, but officials found 66. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office eventually admitted that three of the extra automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) were theirs but didn't explain how or why they deployed them without a permit, leaving 11 that no one, including the county's other two police departments, has claimed.
ALPRs like those from Flock and Axon use AI to read license plates from passing vehicles and automatically sort them into a searchable database, which authorities can use to track movements. When the cameras flag license plates connected to crimes or investigations (sometimes in error), officers can stop and search the vehicles without a warrant.
Obvious worries about mass surveillance have prompted hundreds of communities across the US to end their contracts with Flock, though it claims new contracts far outpace cancelations. Another concern is misuse by police – dozens of officers have been caught using ALPRs for stalking. In many places, citizens have taken it upon themselves to destroy the cameras.
St. Lucie County has covered the unclaimed cameras in plastic for the time being, attaching notices that officials will remove them in 30 days, a deadline that could expire between October 16 and October 20. One camera has already mysteriously disappeared, according to The Washington Post.
Concerningly, Flock cameras aren't necessarily exclusive to police departments and don't always require government permits. While Flock usually conducts permit negotiations and installations, private companies can sign contracts with the manufacturer, and a spokesperson confirmed they can place ALPRs in certain locations without permits.
Flock has installed cameras in several other states and communities without permits over the past few years, some on behalf of unknown clients. When Grass Valley, California, recently removed its ALPRs, Flock reinstalled some of them without informing officials.
In response to pushback, the company has placed greater restrictions on police database searches. By the end of the year, searches will require entering case numbers, but authorities can bypass the step in emergencies. A Florida congressman also recently introduced a bill that would require warrants to use ALPRs.

articles.title: I tested the first eco-friendly phone offered to US buyers in years — I just wish it wasn't so expensive
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Fairphone 6 Plus isn't competitively priced, but it promises to be an eco-friendly phone — and one that's available, notably, in the US. Some neat design features and a rugged build are highlights, but the specs on offer here are relatively mid-range and lag behind rivals' offerings. The real competitor to the Fairphone 6 Plus is its regular sibling, as this 'Plus' model doesn't offer much that's new besides a higher price point.
Reasons to buy
- + Built to last
- + Responsive fingerprint scanner
- + Solid green credentials
Reasons to avoid
- - Bulky chassis
- - Modest upgrade over the Fairphone 6
- - High price for specs
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Fairphone 6 Plus: Two-minute review
To many in Europe, Fairphone is seen as a niche yet reliable Android manufacturer that specializes in one thing: fair phones. Its devices are made from eco-friendly materials, in factories that respect their workers, and are designed to last ages so they don't become e-waste.
But the new Fairphone 6 Plus — officially called the Fairphone Gen 6 Plus — is not just for European buyers. It's the first of the Dutch brand's smartphones to be released in the US, giving a whole new audience of green-minded consumers the chance to buy a phone that aligns with their ethical beliefs.
If that's you, the Fairphone 6's slightly newer successor is an easy recommendation; there's no real competition in the environmentally-friendly phone space, at least since Teracube stopped making new devices. But there are other reasons to pick up the Fairphone 6 Plus, too.
For starters, it boasts impressive durability credentials, with a military-grade chassis and plastic body that shrugs off drops and bumps with ease. If you do damage something, the phone is easy to open up at home, allowing you to replace parts instead of throwing the device away or shelling out loads of money for a company to repair it.
In fact, that's Fairphone's whole schtick: it wants your phone to last as long as possible, to avoid it going into landfill (they're eco-friendly, remember). So the 7 years of software updates make sense too.
Okay, so you're now brushed up on Fairphone, but let's fully rip the band-aid off: the brand's phones are rarely good value for money if you compare them with similarly priced rivals. It's the same with Fairphone's audio products, like the Fairbuds XL: you pay for longevity, not features.
Samsung, Google, and Motorola all offer Fairphone 6 Plus-beating phones for the same price, and if you live outside the US, a whole host of Chinese brands offer superior specs for a fraction of the cost. The Fairphone 6 Plus doesn't match its rivals in performance, camera capabilities, or slimness (though longevity, of course, is a different conversation).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Normally with Fairphones, you're paying for their eco-friendly credentials and high level of repairability. But a price hike for the Fairphone 6 Plus over the non-Plus model makes this trade-off a little harder to stomach, especially when the specs are barely different. And sure, price hikes are rife these days — Fairphone isn't alone in charging more for not much more — but they're harder to justify when the handsets weren't that competitive anyway.
But that 4-star score? As a devout green buyer, I'd still recommend the Fairphone 6 Plus. It lets you talk the talk and walk the walk, as long as you don't need a flagship phone. For me, Fairphone is the only company whose tech is actually, genuinely green — there's no greenwashing going on here (at least to my knowledge).
Still, the Fairphone 6 Plus is only worth it if you have the money to spare, plan on keeping your handset for a long time, or find it discounted in the sales. And if it is on sale in your country, keep tabs on the Fairphone 6 too: it's basically the same phone for a slightly lower price.
Fairphone 6 Plus review: price and availability
- Released in August 2026 in Europe and US
- Sells for $649.99 / £569 (roughly AU$1,100)
- Price hike over predecessor
The Fairphone 6 Plus was revealed in mid-August 2026, a little over a year after the unveiling of the ‘standard’ or non-Plus model. This is Fairphone’s modus operandi: it often releases main-series phones every other year, bridging the gap with ‘Plus’ models in the meantime.
This latest Plus model justifies that suffix with its price, though. The Fairphone 6 Plus costs $649.99 / £569 (roughly AU$1,100, though Fairphone doesn’t sell its tech in Australia), which is a sizeable price hike over the Fairphone 6’s £499 (roughly $680 / AU$990) starting price. The latter phone remains on sale as a valid alternative to the newer handset, especially for cost-conscious buyers.
Given the relatively few upgrades the new model offers, for a higher price, its value proposition just isn’t as competitive.
Notice how I could share a US price for the Fairphone 6 Plus? That's because it's the first of the brand’s mobiles to be sold in the States, finally giving green-minded US buyers a phone to buy since Teracube went quiet.
As I'll mention later in the review, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed to be repaired, and you can easily buy spare parts on the brand's websites. These range in price and vary by region, and so instead of reeling off a massive list, I'll simply refer you to Fairphone's website for the full list.
It's worth noting, too, that the Fairphone 6 Plus — like many previous Fairphone models — is also available in a de-Googled /e/OS configuration from Murena, which puts privacy at the forefront of the experience. This version of the phone costs $699.99 / £599 (around AU$1,009). We'll be publishing a separate feature on the de-Googled Fairphone experience in the coming weeks.
Fairphone 6 Plus review: specs
| Fairphone 6 Plus specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Specs | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions: | 156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mm | 
| Weight: | 193g | 
| Screen: | 6.31-inch FHD (1,116 x 2,484mm) 120Hz OLED | 
| Chipset: | Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 |

| Primary camera: | 50MP, f/1.9 |

Fairphone 6 Plus review: design
- Bulky handset that stretches the hand
- Neat touches like a switch, a side-mounted fingerprint scanner, and military protection
- Easily repairable and modifiable
People often turn their noses up at Fairphones for their middling specs, but I’ve used most of them, and to me, I'd say their designs are an equal reason why some users may be put off. These phones are bulky. The 6 Plus measures 156.5 x 73.3 x 9.6mm and weighs 193g, so in this age of super-slim mobiles, it feels like a dinosaur.
There are benefits to this chunky size. Not only does it ensure the phone is easier to repair — more on that later — but it means it's better protected too. Case in point, the Fairphone 6 Plus has the military-grade MIL-STD-810H compliance, and IP55 protection against dust and water jets. I used the handset without a case and never felt like it was at risk.
On the left edge of the phone you get your power rocker, and on the right there’s a power button with a fingerprint scanner embedded. This worked flawlessly in my testing, unlocking the handset instantly and never failing to recognise my thumb, though some prefer phones with under-display scanners.
The right edge also has a physical switch, which can be programmed for different functions like turning on Airplane mode, enabling the torch, or enabling Fairphone’s Moments (which basically turns your handset into a ‘Lite’ mode with only access to certain apps). The switch is useful if you use it right, but it’s a shame that the list of functions is a little limited. I can’t use it to instantly open Google Maps, for example, or turn on NFC.
You can buy the mobile in a fetching blue, as you can see in the images, which is new for the Plus model. There are also green and black options, matching the Fairphone 6’s hues (but no white, as was offered for the previous model).
Now onto one of the big draws of Fairphone handsets: they’re designed to be repairable. This means you can remove various elements using a simple Fairphone screwdriver, and replace them if anything is damaged. If you smash the screen of your handset, scratch the lens, or find the battery health greatly diminished, you can simply swap the offending components out instead of buying an entirely new phone.
A side-effect of this modularity, which Fairphone has greatly leaned on in recent years, is that you can remove the parts for another purpose: buying accessories. You can swap out the phone’s back and replace it with a card holder or finger loop, for instance, the latter of which you can see in all of these review pictures (I absolutely love using it to hold the phone).
There are other accessories available from the My Fairphone app, and they all vary in price.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Fairphone 6 Plus review: display
- 6.31 inches, 1,116 x 2,484 resolution
- 120Hz refresh rate, 1,400 nits max brightness
- Decent display, but nothing special
Despite the Fairphone 6 Plus feeling like a pretty chunky phone in the hand, its display is a little smaller than those of many Android rivals.
The panel measures 6.31 inches diagonally, and it's broken up by a top-center punch-hole cut-out for the front camera. It's got a 1116 x 2484 resolution, 120Hz refresh rate, and 20:9 aspect ratio; the size, OLED build, and 1400-nit max brightness all match the specs of the Fairphone 6’s panel.
A note on the refresh rate: by default, it’s set to 90Hz, so bump it up in the Settings app if you don’t mind the resulting lower battery life.
I can’t pretend that this is the best-looking screen on any Android phone, but the difference between ‘best’ and ‘good enough’ is tiny, and the Fairphone 6 Plus’ display will seem as good as any other to most users. Unless you’re doing something wild like professional photo editing, you’ll find the display to be bright and responsive.
One small annoyance: at the top of the display is a speaker grille, which is much larger than most you see in this day and age. It proved quite the fluff magnet when the phone was in my pocket; I kept having to pick bits of tissue out of it.
- Display score: 4 / 5
Fairphone 6 Plus review: software
- Stock Android 16 (or /e/OS in alternative model)
- And I mean stock: there's no bloatware or extra features
- Seven years of OS updates
The Fairphone 6 Plus comes with Android 16 pre-installed — and I mean stock Android, not ‘almost-stock’ like some other brands use. So you’re not getting loads of random pre-installed social media and holiday apps here. There's a single pre-installed app (which I'll get to later), and beyond that, you’re getting a clean slate with the bare minimum Google apps that all Android phones come equipped with.
A clean interface is great, but you’re also lacking other brands’ customization options here. If you like tweaking the look of your phone until it’s truly unique, you’ll find the Fairphone lacking — though I’ll applaud the accessibility options like high-contrast icons and text outlines that make writing easier to read.
Otherwise, you’re getting the ‘standard’ Android experience: a home screen in which to bury apps, widgets and shortcuts, plus a familiar quick-settings menu if you swipe down from the top of the phone, though I occasionally faced a recurring bug that wouldn’t let me close it easily. I also missed Circle to Search, a close-to-universal Android feature that isn’t available on Fairphones.
This aforementioned extra app is My Fairphone, which you won’t be using all the time, so you can hide it in the App Gallery. It lets you check your phone’s health (including storage use, temperature, and runtime since last reboot), and buy accessories or spare parts for your phone. If you’re planning to keep your Fairphone running for years, this latter option will be the most intriguing — although some may find the My Fairphone app unnecessary.
Fairphone has pledged that its Gen 6 Plus phone will get at least seven Android updates (bringing you to Android 24, if Google’s software naming stays true), which is one of the best commitments we’ve seen for Androids. It helps the company's longevity promise; this phone will keep working for a long time.
Not sure about using Google’s hegemonic operating system? A version of the phone is available with /e/OS, an open-source ‘anti-Android’ operating system designed around data control, privacy and security. Given that it’s not Android, it’s not designed for the average buyer, but some people who want something more secure might consider it. However, I haven’t tested it, so I can’t give a personal take on how it works.
- Software score: 4.5 / 5
Fairphone 6 Plus review: cameras
- 50MP main, 13MP ultra-wide, and 32MP front cameras
- Basic, expected range of camera modes
- Very light-touch optimization (perhaps too light-touch)
Fairphone decided to keep its camera array unchanged from the Fairphone 6 to the new model, which means I'm going to keep my camera score similarly unchanged.
We're looking at a 50MP f/1.9 main and 13MP f/2.2 rear duo, with a 32MP f/2.0 front-facing camera rounding out the party. Okay, there's been one tweak: the main snapper now has a smaller aperture, but the changes aren't huge.
I wouldn't recommend a Fairphone if you're looking for an accomplished camera phone, and as the unchanged specs show, the 6 Plus hasn't changed my stance. It's totally fine for the average buyer — your holiday snaps or selfies will be perfectly acceptable — but you won't be taking anything particularly amazing.
You can see this from the camera samples below, and the handicap is that the image optimization isn't particularly game-changing. Look at the field of flowers, or pizza: another handset would add much more saturation and contrast. The phone can perform better, but only in really well-lit scenarios. But, as I keep saying, its cameras are mostly fine. You can drop your photos into Photoshop if you want, to make up the difference.
The Fairphone 6 Plus offers the expected range of modes, including Portrait, low-light Night mode, and a Pro mode, but there's nothing especially unique, as you'd find in a Samsung or Google Pixel device.
I took the Fairphone on vacation, and the one thing I really missed was a way to zoom in. You can use digital zoom up to 10x, but anything over 2x looks a little too grainy to use. I would've loved to see a dedicated zoom lens added to this phone, but those only show up on devices designed for photography (or phones that cost significantly more).
- Camera score: 3.5 / 5

Fairphone 6 Plus review: performance and audio
- Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 chip, 12GB RAM, and 256GB storage
- Mid-range performance, though it starts sluggishly
- Bluetooth 6.0 but no headphone jack
Arguably the main Fairphone 6 Plus upgrade versus its regular sibling is its performance. The RAM capacity is up to 12GB (something I asked for in my review of the Fairphone 6), and the chipset is now a Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 (the previous model had a Gen 3). That’s the same chipset as you'll find inside the Nothing Phone (4a), so it’s no slouch on the performance front.
I’ve previously found the Snapdragon 7-series chips to be fine for mid-range devices like this, and the Fairphone 6 Plus is no exception — even if it did struggle now and then to run certain games. Most users will find it enough for most tasks, though this isn’t really a device designed for gamers.
When I put the phone through benchmarking tests, it returned an average Geekbench 7 multi-core score of around 3,500. Geekbench 7 is fairly new, so we haven't used it on enough phones to give useful comparisons, but the tool's browser library suggests this is a similar result to other mid-range mobiles.
On 3DMark, I put the phone through various tests. The results showed that the handset lags quite far behind flagships, even ones from several years ago, but it does stand as more powerful than the 'standard' Fairphone 6.
Just bought the Fairphone 6 Plus and finding it surprisingly slow? Most mobiles take a little while to get up to speed, but mine took a few days more than I’m used to. Give it some time before you declare something’s wrong.
Like most phones, the Fairphone has stereo speakers and no 3.5mm jack, so you’ll probably be relying on its Bluetooth 5.4 support for audio. One minor upgrade from past models is that the device supports aptX Lossless, so in theory, it’s better for audiophiles, but it still doesn’t support LDAC, so this is only a small win.
- Performance score: 3.5 / 5
Fairphone 6 Plus review: battery life
- Relatively small 4,415mAh battery
- Lasts roughly a day of use
- 30W charging, no wireless or reverse powering
The Fairphone 6 Plus has a 4,415mAh battery — on paper, that’s a little lower than most contemporaries, which usually offer power packs of 5,000mAh or above. However, in the past, I’ve been wowed by the battery life of Fairphone devices, which have often outperformed their spec sheets.
Not so much in the 6 Plus. Its battery life is ‘fine’, but the RAM and chipset upgrades from the past model clearly take their toll. The Fairphone lasts for about a day of average use, which is nothing to turn your nose up at, but it’s nothing exceptional, either. When I took the device on holiday, I relied on battery saver mode to make sure I had all the juice I needed.
You can power the phone up at 30W, which isn’t especially fast, but since fast charging can adversely affect battery health, it’s a hard thing to be critical of. You’ll have to plug the phone in for over an hour to charge it to full. There’s also no wireless or reverse power functionality.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Fairphone 6 Plus review: value
I have the same problem every time I review a Fairphone; any other device with the same specs would cost a lot less, but with a Fairphone, you’re buying a device that lasts longer than rivals and takes much less of a toll on the environment.
Does that mean they’re good value or not? Because of their longevity, I usually say 'yes'. Fairphones aren't cheap, but if they last you twice as long as a rival phone would, and you’d end up buying two alternatives instead of one Fairphone, the price is justified.
But the Fairphone 6 Plus' price hike over the Fairphone 6 gives me pause to second-guess this. This phone is still a green marvel that will keep ticking for years, but its high price will probably deter most people from picking it up — and that's a shame.
- Value score: 3.5 / 5
Should you buy the Fairphone 6 Plus?
| Fairphone 6 Plus scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | The Fairphone will last a long time, but the upfront cost is a barrier to entry. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Design | The device may look rough and rugged, but its repairability and hardiness mostly make up for it. | 4 / 5 | 
| Display | The Fairphone's screen matches most rivals at this price: it looks pretty good. | 4 / 5 | 
| Software | Android here is nice and basic: no bloatware, no excess. The 7 years of guaranteed software updates ensure the handset's longevity. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Camera | The cameras aren't terrible, but this phone isn't designed for photography. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | While the chip and RAM are fit for purpose, this isn't a gaming phone. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Battery | At a day of lasting power, you're basically getting the average Android battery life here. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You care about the planet
It's the whole point of the Fairphone 6 Plus, and the reason you've got this far in the review. This is the unbeaten eco-friendly handset.
You want something that lasts a long time
Between its hardy build, repairable nature, and long software span, this is a phone you'll keep for years and years, not something to upgrade the next time a new model is released.
You like side fingerprint scanners
They're pretty rare nowadays, but many people (myself included) prefer side-mounted fingerprint scanners. Thankfully, the Fairphone 6 Plus has one.
Don't buy it if...
You need a gaming or photography phone
The Fairphone 6 Plus is a jack of all trades, but a master of none, and that includes both gaming and photography. Buy a different phone if you need something solid in those areas.
You can buy the Fairphone 6
I hate to disparage a Fairphone, but the older phone is cheaper, and almost equal in specs to this new model.
Fairphone 6 Plus review: Also consider
Not convinced by Fairphone's latest eco-phone? Here are some alternatives, all of which ostensibly have a green angle.
Fairphone 6
I've mentioned it enough in this review. The Fairphone 6 is slightly weaker but costs less, and has all the same eco credentials as the Plus model.
Read our full Fairphone 6 review
HMD Fusion
It's a bit older, so much so that it's no longer receiving software updates, but a lot cheaper. This HMD phone is designed to be easily repairable, and it's also modular with attachable back plates. According to iFixit, its repairability is second only to the Fairphone. Its specs aren't great, though.
iPhone 17
Apple's iPhones aren't eco-friendly by any stretch of the imagination, but lots of their components are recycled, which is better than nothing. Plus, the packaging avoids plastics.

How I tested the Fairphone 6 Plus
- Tested for one month
- Everyday usage, including web browsing, social media, photography, video calling, gaming, streaming video, music playback

To write this Fairphone 6 Plus review, I used the device for one month. I conducted lab-style testing during one week of this month-long period, but for the other three weeks, I popped my SIM into the 6 Plus and used it as my normal smartphone.
This means I used it for texting, playing games, streaming music, working, and taking pictures as anyone else would. During this time, I also used the 6 Plus abroad during a vacation, so it really got put through its paces.
I've been reviewing Android phones for TechRadar since the start of 2019, and was on the team for much of that time. This means I've tested plenty of other competitors and past Fairphone models (including the Fairphone 6), as well as some other gadgets from the company, including its headphones.
I also recently published a long-read piece on gadget repairability for TechRadar, which included an interview with Fairphone's Head of Product.

articles.title: Denmark’s Breye Therapeutics raises €67.5 million to advance oral therapies for early treatment of retinal diseases | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Breye Therapeutics (Breye), a Danish clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing oral therapeutics for the early treatment of retinal diseases, has closed an oversubscribed €67.5 million Series A financing round.
The round was co-led by new investor Mission BioCapital and existing investor Novo Holdings, with participation from existing investor Sound Bioventures and additional new investors, including the Ljungström family office, Innovestor Life Science, EIFO, Catalyze Capital, Modi Ventures and Pappas Capital. Together with this financing, Robert Blazej, Partner at Mission BioCapital, and Lukas Ljungström from the Ljungström family office will join Breye’s board.
Ulrik Mouritzen, Chief Executive Officer, Breye Therapeutics, said, “This €67.5 million Series A financing, which includes significant support from both new and existing investors, reflects the strong confidence in Breye’s vision, strategy, and pipeline. It marks a major milestone for the Company and validates the enormous progress we have made to date. Importantly, it enables us to advance danegaptide, our pioneering, first-in-class oral treatment for diabetic retinopathy, to the next stage of clinical development – bringing a much-needed patient-friendly treatment option closer to those living with this debilitating eye disease.”
Breye was founded in 2019 and emerged from stealth in November 2022 after closing a €4 million Seed round led by Novo Holdings and Sound Bioventures. Mouritzen, an M.D. and industry veteran with more than 20 years of R&D, regulatory, and commercial experience in Europe and the US, leads the company.
It is developing a pipeline of oral therapies for eye diseases, such as intermediate age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma. According to the company, diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision loss among working-age adults, affecting about 130 million people worldwide today. It also highlighted that the current market value of diabetic retinopathy therapeutics is approaching €8.8 billion ($10 billion), and could nearly double over the next decade, with a predicted CAGR of 6.5%.
“While currently available intravitreal (IVT) treatments can help preserve vision in patients with late-stage disease, their invasive nature – being injected directly into the eye – means they are often poorly tolerated and associated with low continued adherence. In addition, treatment options for patients with early- or moderate-stage Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) remain very limited,” the company mentioned in the press release.
It opines that this unmet medical need, coupled with a growing patient population, highlights the substantial market opportunity for danegaptide.
Danegaptide is the company’s lead candidate and a first-in-class oral small molecule with a novel mechanism of action that stabilises retinal vasculature, protecting against retinal capillary breakdown and vascular leakage caused by chronically high glucose levels (hyperglycemia).
Breye reports that the financing follows the successful completion of a Phase 1b trial in patients with NPDR last year, which showed danegaptide was well tolerated across all dose levels and exhibited early signs of clinical activity, including retinal imaging data consistent with reductions in vascular leakage, one of the core pathologies of NPDR.
Recently, Breye also published an academic paper analysing the pre-clinical and early clinical-stage evidence for danegaptide in the prestigious journal Science Translational Medicine.
Robert Blazej, Partner, Mission BioCapital, said, “Breye is emerging as a leader in the development of innovative retinal disease therapies, as demonstrated by the promising results from its recent Phase Ib study of danegaptide, and we are excited to support the Company at this pivotal stage of growth. With its highly differentiated approach, clear development strategy and experienced team, we believe Breye is uniquely positioned to address a significant unmet need in diabetic retinopathy.”
The company plans to use this capital to advance Breye’s lead asset danegaptide into a randomised Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with NPDR. The study, which aims to demonstrate clinical proof of concept, is due to start in 2027.
The funding will also support the company’s broader pipeline of oral small molecules, including a P2X7 receptor antagonist for iAMD intended to reduce nerve damage and inflammation, and additional glaucoma candidates with neuroprotective effects. These are advancing towards IND-enabling studies.

articles.title: La guerre entre Google Meet et Microsoft Teams vient de prendre un virage inattendu
articles.text:
Arriver dans une salle de réunion et constater que le boîtier tourne sur Google Meet alors que le lien reçu est un rendez-vous Microsoft Teams provoque généralement un petit vent de panique. Jusqu’ici, la solution était donc de squatter un ordinateur portable ou de déménager tout le monde en catastrophe dans la bonne salle. La nouvelle interopérabilité entre les deux écosystèmes sur le matériel de visioconférence devrait grandement aider.
La fin des frontières entre plateformes de visio
Déployée progressivement depuis le 1er octobre, cette mise à jour permet aux salles équipées de matériel Google Meet de rejoindre sans problème des réunions hébergées sur Microsoft Teams. La réciproque fonctionne aussi pour les Microsoft Teams Rooms tournant sous Android, qui acceptent désormais les appels lancés depuis Google Meet. Concrètement, si une entreprise utilise principalement les outils de Google au quotidien, mais reçoit un lien Teams de la part d’un client externe, le boîtier de la salle gère l’appel tiers directement. Plus personne n’a besoin de brancher des câbles dans tous les sens pour afficher l’image sur l’écran principal.
Un déploiement automatique sous le contrôle des admins
Cette nouveauté arrive directement sur les appareils sans manipulation particulière de la part des utilisateurs. Le déploiement se fait sur trois jours. Du côté des administrateurs réseau, la fonction s’active par défaut, tout en gardant la possibilité d’être désactivée au niveau de chaque unité si la politique interne de l’entreprise l’exige. Une nouveauté qui devrait retirer une belle épine du pied à tous ceux qui utilisent régulièrement les deux plateformes.

articles.title: Microsoft prometió un Windows 11 con menos IA, pero la actualización 2026 añade más funciones y no las puedes desactivar
articles.text:
Windows 11 ha liberado su actualización de 2026 con nuevas funciones y algunos de los ajustes más pedidos por los usuarios. Pese a que Microsoft cumplió en algunos apartados, la empresa no quita el dedo del renglón y sigue añadiendo funciones de inteligencia artificial. En el peor de los casos, la empresa las presenta como un motivo para instalar la versión 26H2 hoy mismo.
De acuerdo con Neowin, el caso más evidente de esta estrategia es el agente que encontramos en Configuración, el cual sustituye la búsqueda clásica por una IA que encuentra las cosas por ti. Si quieres realizar un ajuste específico y no sabes en dónde se encuentra, basta con pedírselo usando lenguaje natural y lo hará por ti. Esto suena bien para un usuario principiante, pero para aquellos que llevan años con Windows y quieren hacer las cosas por su cuenta, deshabilitar el agente no es una opción viable.
Existe una herramienta llamada Editor de directivas de grupo que es útil para desactivar funciones que no tienen un interruptor en Windows. Aunque Microsoft la diseñó para administradores de sistemas, los usuarios entusiastas con Windows 11 Pro también le sacan provecho. En el caso del asistente de IA de Configuración, Microsoft añadió una directiva llamada DisableSettingsAgent, que elimina esa experiencia y deja solo la búsqueda indexada y semántica.
Lamentablemente, esa opción solo está disponible para las versiones de Windows 11 Enterprise, IoT Enterprise y Educación. Los usuarios con Windows 11 Pro no pueden deshabilitar el agente ni crear una entrada en el registro de forma manual.
Tomando en cuenta que la mayoría de los equipos para consumidores se vende con las versiones Home y Pro, el uso del agente será casi obligatorio para los ordenadores compatibles con IA.
Windows 11 no se olvidará de la IA
Otra función es la de los conectores que permiten a los agentes de IA controlar tu PC, acceder a archivos, ajustes y otras capacidades del sistema. En el Explorador de archivos, por ejemplo, un agente puede leer, crear y modificar archivos locales, siempre y cuando tenga un permiso explícito.
Si quieres apagar estos conectores por completo y tienes Windows 11 Home o Pro, lamentablemente no podrás hacerlo, ya que esta opción solo está disponible para las versiones Enterprise, IoT Enterprise y Educación del sistema operativo. El reporte menciona que algunas de estas directivas siguen vinculadas a compilaciones Insider, por lo que Microsoft podría modificar la compatibilidad antes de que lleguen a todos los usuarios.
Algunos dirán que esto es lo que se obtiene por creerse el cuento de la IA y comprarse un Copilot+ PC. Cierto o no, Microsoft debería ofrecer una opción para deshabilitar estas características, sobre todo permitir que los usuarios puedan desactivar los conectores MCP o limitar a qué servidores y hosts pueden conectarse los agentes. Los usuarios de Windows 11 Home son los más afectados por no poder modificar las directivas de grupo, aunque existe la opción de crear a mano las entradas en el registro (siempre y cuando Microsoft las respete).
En contraste, existen funciones que sí son opcionales. La primera de ellas es la memoria fotográfica de Recall, que tanta polémica causó y su retraso terminó por matar el concepto de las Copilot+ PC. Si no te interesa, puedes desactivarla a través de un interruptor en las opciones, al igual que Click to Do, esa herramienta que ofrece acciones rápidas sobre el contenido de la pantalla.
Para los usuarios con un ordenador convencional, Copilot es una app común y corriente que puede desinstalarse desde la Configuración.

articles.title: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to become Skydance | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will operate as Skydance once their merger closes, Paramount CEO David Ellison announced Friday. Skydance is the name of Ellison’s original film production company.
The roughly $110 billion deal is expected to close October 6. It will combine two major Hollywood studios, Paramount+ and HBO Max, and networks including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network. Skydance will also control franchises such as “The Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” the DC Universe, and “Yellowstone.”
The merger followed a drawn-out corporate battle. Netflix had agreed to acquire Warner Bros.’ streaming and studio businesses before the broader Paramount deal moved forward. Twelve states challenged the deal, arguing it could reduce competition and harm consumers and workers, but a judge approved a settlement with the state attorneys general this week.
Ellison said the Paramount and Warner Bros. brands will remain central. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one,” he wrote on X. The new name, he said, gives the company “an identity of its own” while letting both studios “remain in the spotlight.”

articles.title: GitHub's advice for its new Copilot feature is to try something else first
articles.text:
GitHub’s advice for its new Copilot feature is to try something else first
GitHub launched computer use in public preview on Thursday, giving Copilot CLI and its desktop app the ability to operate applications on macOS and Windows. Agents can read app content and click, type, scroll, and drag, including in older, GUI-only software with no API, command-line interface, or MCP integration.
An expense report in Safari was GitHub’s launch demonstration but the company described other uses including summarizing information in a legacy application, updating a presentation, entering data, and moving information between apps. Developers can access the feature from the terminal or through the Copilot app, which runs on Copilot CLI and launched earlier this year as a rival to Claude Code and Codex.
GitHub has some catching up to do. OpenAI added computer use to Codex in April, while Anthropic brought broader computer use on macOS to Claude Code and Claude Cowork earlier this year.
GitHub has some catching up to do.
Computer use vs. MCP servers
Enabling computer use in Copilot CLI activates a bundled plugin with its own MCP server. It works in local sessions, reading application content through the operating system’s accessibility tree and taking screenshots when it needs visual context.
The company recommends using direct tools wherever possible. So, if an API, MCP server, terminal command, filesystem tool, or dedicated browser tool can handle the task, it typically provides more structured information and more predictable results than desktop interaction.
That advice limits where GitHub thinks computer use belongs. OpenAI president Greg Brockman made a broader case last month, arguing that agents could use the same interfaces as people and spare the industry the work of building and maintaining a connector for every piece of software.
Saved approvals outlast their removal
Developers enable the feature with /computer on in Copilot CLI or through the Copilot app’s Computer Use settings. macOS also requires Accessibility permission to operate controls and Screen Recording permission to inspect windows when visual context is needed.
The CLI session’s permission mode determines whether Copilot asks before accessing an app; developers can check it with /permissions show. When prompted, they can allow access for the current session, choose “Always allow” for future sessions or decline. Deny rules override both automatic and saved approvals.
Approvals saved in the CLI carry over to the desktop app on the same computer. Removing an app from the always-allowed list clears its approval for future sessions but leaves access already granted in a running session intact.
Stopping work requires a separate action: press Esc twice in the CLI, or click Stop or press Esc in the desktop app.
Enterprise controls over computer use
Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference. If managed settings block computer use, Copilot CLI reports that the feature is unavailable.
Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference.
Through managed-settings.json, enterprise owners can also control whether developers may bypass approval prompts. That restriction applies across the Copilot app, CLI, and VS Code.
GitHub’s default-enablement policy for Business and Enterprise does not change this preview’s opt-in status. The policy starts applying to unconfigured features on October 22 but excludes preview features.
Reliability depends on the interface
A change in timing or window state can cause Copilot to repeat an action or stall. GitHub also warns that the agent may choose the wrong control, type into the wrong field, or struggle with dynamic interfaces and complex workflows.
Sensitive information visible in an application window may also become context for the agent.
Unexpected on-screen content and ambiguous instructions can lead to actions affecting the user’s device, data, or connected accounts. Sensitive information visible in an application window may also become context for the agent.

articles.title: Judge dismisses antitrust lawsuits over Google AI Overviews
articles.text:
Google has won a dismissal of two lawsuits alleging that the company’s AI Overviews in Search negatively impact internet traffic.
Last year, news publisher Penske Media Corporation (PMC) and ed tech company Chegg filed antitrust lawsuits against Google, arguing that the search giant’s AI Overviews were drawing people away from their sites. Google naturally filed to dismiss the suits, and on Oct. 1, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ultimately ruled in favour of Google.
In court, Mehta said AI Overviews don’t violate antitrust law as neither Penske nor Chegg had formal agreements with Google.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.”
That said, Mehta, who was the same judge who ruled in 2024 that Google operates a search monopoly, did acknowledge that Google’s AI search features is harming publishers.
“The court does not treat Plaintiffs’ alleged harms lightly,” he wrote. “Nor is it unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in, and the knock-on consequences to journalists, educators, and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation.”
Indeed, there has been a lot of research from groups like the Pew Research Institute that demonstrates that AI Overviews can siphon as much as 50 per cent — if not more — of traffic from websites. That’s to say nothing of the misinformation that AI Overviews continues to spread. But of course, Mehta’s job was simply to determine whether Google’s harmful AI tools actually broke any laws, and ultimately, he concluded that wasn’t the case.
Image credit: Google
Source: United States District Court Via: Engadget

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered a un problème de cheveux, Mercredi a déjà sa saison 3, et le speedrun de Metal Gear Solid 2 évolue : c'est le récap pop culture de la semaine
articles.text:
CD Projekt Red recommande de désactiver une option graphique dans The Witcher 3
- Le support technique de CD Projekt Red conseille de désactiver l’option Nvidia HairWorks dans la version Remastered de The Witcher 3 pour éviter des problèmes de performance en attendant un correctif.
- La technologie Nvidia HairWorks, malgré son potentiel à améliorer l’esthétique des jeux vidéo, est critiquée depuis plus de 11 ans pour son impact négatif sur les performances, notamment sur les cartes graphiques AMD.
- Même les configurations haut de gamme rencontrent des baisses significatives de framerate avec HairWorks activé, démontrant la persistance des problèmes d’optimisation.
Mercredi saison 3 avance vite et la série Netflix franchit une grosse étape
- Netflix a officialisé la fin du tournage de la saison 3 de Mercredi en partageant une photo inédite de Jenna Ortega sur le plateau accompagnée du message « Season 3 has officially wrapped ».
- La saison 3 étoffe la distribution avec des recrues de poids comme Eva Green, Winona Ryder (dans le rôle inédit de Tabitha), Lena Headey, Andrew McCarthy et James Lance.
- Entrée en post‑production, la saison est désormais pressentie pour une sortie à l’automne 2027, Netflix n’ayant pas encore fixé de date officielle.
Un joueur de Metal Gear Solid 2 a fait une découverte historique
- apel, un speedrunner chevronné, a découvert un exploit dans Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty qui permet d’éviter le premier combat contre le boss Olga, une première en 25 ans d’histoire du jeu.
- Cette technique, nommée « Olga Skip », utilise un garde endormi pour déclencher les explosifs sans les réarmer, permettant à Snake de franchir un couloir piégé.

articles.title: Öffentliches WLAN absichern: Wie Androids Private DNS deine Daten schützt
articles.text:
Private DNS auf Android: So schützt du dich im öffentlichen WLAN
Wenn der eigene mobile Hotspot nicht ausreicht, können öffentliche WLAN-Netzwerke eine praktische Alternative sein, um E-Mails zu bearbeiten oder sich beim Warten auf den Flieger die Zeit zu vertreiben. Es gibt allerdings einen Haken: Diese öffentlichen Netzwerke sind nämlich oft nicht ausreichend abgesichert. Genau hierfür bietet Android die integrierte „Privates DNS”-Funktion, die einen entscheidenden Teil der Verbindung verschlüsselt.
Bei öffentlichem WLAN ist Vorsicht geboten
Eigentlich gehen Menschen in Deutschland eher sorgsam mit ihren Daten um. Bei öffentlichen WLAN-Netzwerken scheint diese Vorsicht aber oft zu enden. Laut einer Umfrage des eSIM-Anbieters Saily nutzen 71 Prozent der Deutschen auf Reisen öffentliches WLAN. Gemeinsam mit dem Vereinigten Königreich liegt Deutschland damit im Vergleich an der Spitze. Reisende aus Spanien oder den USA zeigten sich zurückhaltender. Das Problem: In solchen Netzwerken können andere potenziell mitlesen, welche Seiten Nutzer:innen aufrufen, oder sie unbemerkt auf gefälschte Anmeldeseiten umleiten.
Wenn jemand auf einen Link tippt oder eine App öffnet, muss das Smartphone zunächst herausfinden, wo sich die Website oder der Dienst befindet. Diese Aufgabe übernimmt das Domain Name System (DNS), das Internet- in IP-Adressen übersetzt. Da DNS zu den ältesten Bestandteilen des Internets gehört, wurde es allerdings nicht mit Blick auf den Datenschutz entwickelt. Anfragen laufen unverschlüsselt, sodass theoretisch jede Person mitlesen kann. Im Heimnetz ist das meist nur der Internetanbieter, in öffentlichen Netzen gilt das potenziell für deutlich mehr Personen – und nicht alle davon haben gute Absichten.
So lässt sich Private DNS auf Android einrichten
Private DNS kann dieses Problem lösen. Google hat die Funktion mit Android 9 Pie eingeführt. Seitdem ist sie fester Bestandteil jeder Version. Android nutzt dafür DNS-over-TLS – dabei werden Abfragen mit derselben Verschlüsselung geschützt wie HTTPS-Websites. Das Smartphone baut eine sichere Verbindung zu einem vertrauenswürdigen Resolver auf, prüft dessen Identität und sendet Abfragen darüber. Andere können den DNS-Verkehr so nicht mehr mitlesen. Private DNS hat allerdings seine Grenzen: Es verbirgt weder die IP-Adresse noch ersetzt es ein VPN. Dafür schließt es eine häufig ausgenutzte Lücke auf Betriebssystemebene – und zwar ohne, dass zusätzliche Software benötigt wird.
Die Einrichtung dauert weniger als eine Minute und erfordert keine Installation. Auf Pixel-Geräten öffnen Nutzer:innen die Einstellungen, tippen auf „Netzwerk & Internet” und suchen die „Private DNS”-Funktion, die je nach Gerät auch unter „Erweitert” zu finden sein kann. Bei Samsung gibt es die Option unter „Einstellungen”, „Verbindungen” und „Weitere Verbindungseinstellungen”. Dort stehen drei Optionen: Die Option „Automatisch” verschlüsselt nur, wenn der Netzwerk-DNS-Server dies unterstützt – andernfalls greift dein Smartphone unbemerkt auf unverschlüsseltes DNS zurück. Für echten Schutz wählen Nutzer:innen die Option „Hostname des Anbieters” und geben einen Hostnamen anstelle einer IP-Adresse ein. Dadurch nutzt das Smartphone in jedem Netzwerk einen bestimmten verschlüsselten Resolver. Eine beliebte kostenlose Option ist zum Beispiel „dns.google”.
Private DNS ersetzt keinen Rundum-Schutz
Manche öffentlichen Netzwerke, etwa in Hotels oder Unternehmen, blockieren den für DNS-over-TLS nötigen Port. Android warnt dann, dass der Server nicht erreichbar ist, und Seiten laden nicht. Ein vorübergehender Wechsel zu „Automatisch” ist möglich, erfordert aber besondere Vorsicht in diesem Netzwerk. Letztlich kann auch Private DNS ein öffentliches WLAN nicht rundum sicher machen. Die Android-Funktion schließt aber eine beliebte Angriffslücke von Cyberkriminellen. In Kombination mit einem VPN und verantwortungsvollem Verhalten lässt sich ein Android-Smartphone dadurch deutlich schwerer ausspionieren.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 23.09.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

Microsoft Jewel ya se puede jugar en móviles manteniendo el avance alcanzado en PC
articles.text:
Microsoft Jewel ya se puede jugar en móviles manteniendo el avance alcanzado en PC. Microsoft Casual Games lanzó la aplicación como título independiente para iOS y Android, siete años después de su anterior estreno en esta línea de juegos. Se trata del quinto título móvil de la división y permite a los usuarios combinar partidas en el teléfono con las jugadas previamente en computadora, según informó Xbox Wire.
El juego mantiene la mecánica de combinar tres o más piezas que ya existía en Microsoft Solitaire Collection y en la aplicación móvil de Xbox. La diferencia principal está en la posibilidad de sincronizar el progreso entre plataformas y de sumar logros de Xbox directamente desde el celular.
Sincronización de progreso entre móvil y PC
La función que distingue a este lanzamiento es la continuidad del juego entre dispositivos. Un jugador puede iniciar una partida en su teléfono durante un traslado y retomarla luego en la versión para PC sin perder el avance logrado.
Para que esto funcione es necesario iniciar sesión con una cuenta de Microsoft. Ese inicio de sesión es el que permite que el progreso quede guardado en la nube y disponible en cualquiera de las dos versiones, tanto en iOS y Android como en la aplicación independiente para computadora.
Esta sincronización responde a un patrón de uso que combina sesiones cortas con partidas más largas. Según describe Xbox Wire, el formato permite empezar a jugar en minutos libres y continuar cuando se dispone de más tiempo, sin que el dispositivo utilizado sea una limitación para seguir avanzando.
Mecánica de combinar tres joyas y bonificaciones
La jugabilidad se apoya en el esquema clásico de combinar tres o más joyas para eliminarlas del tablero y sumar puntos. Cada movimiento libera espacio y habilita nuevas jugadas, lo que modifica la disposición general del tablero en cada turno.
El título incorpora joyas de bonificación que el jugador puede colocar en puntos estratégicos para maximizar su efecto. A esto se suman potenciadores que permiten generar reacciones en cadena y aumentar la puntuación de forma más rápida.
Microsoft Jewel suma además desafíos diarios, un objetivo que cambia cada jornada y que puede consistir en superar el reto anterior, alcanzar una puntuación más alta o simplemente completar otra ronda de juego.
Logros de Xbox disponibles en dispositivos móviles
Otro de los aportes de esta versión es la posibilidad de desbloquear logros de Xbox jugando desde el teléfono. Hasta ahora, esta función estaba asociada principalmente a la experiencia en PC o en la aplicación móvil de Xbox.
Con el inicio de sesión mediante una cuenta de Microsoft, los jugadores pueden sumar estos logros a su perfil de Xbox sin depender de una consola o computadora. Esto amplía las posibilidades de completar el perfil desde cualquier lugar.
Beneficios para suscriptores de Xbox Game Pass
El lanzamiento también contempla ventajas diferenciadas para los miembros de Xbox Game Pass. Quienes cuenten con esta suscripción acceden a beneficios premium al jugar en PC, entre ellos una experiencia sin publicidad y extras adicionales dentro del propio juego.
En el caso de los suscriptores de Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, esos beneficios premium se extienden tanto a la versión de PC como a la aplicación móvil, de acuerdo con lo detallado por Xbox Wire.
Cómo registrarse en Xbox Game Pass y acceder a su biblioteca de juegos
Para unirte a Xbox Game Pass solo hace falta una cuenta de Microsoft y completar el registro desde una consola Xbox, una computadora con Windows o la aplicación oficial de Xbox.
Al suscribirte, es posible elegir entre las diferentes modalidades disponibles según la plataforma y los beneficios buscados, ya sea para PC, el plan Ultimate o las opciones pensadas para consola. El proceso se completa al cargar un método de pago válido, momento en el que la membresía queda activa de inmediato.
La suscripción se renueva cada mes y otorga acceso a una biblioteca con cientos de títulos disponibles para descargar o para jugar mediante la nube. Entre esos beneficios se incluyen estrenos desde su fecha de lanzamiento y rebajas exclusivas para los miembros.
La gestión de la cuenta queda en manos del usuario en todo momento: desde la sección de servicios del sitio web de la cuenta de Microsoft se puede modificar el plan contratado o cancelar la membresía cuando se desee.

articles.title: White-collar hiring grows 2% led by AI/ML sector in Sep: Report
articles.text:
White-collar hiring grows 2% led by AI/ML sector in Sep: Report
The report revealed that Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) roles continued to record growth, rising 20% in September, while the Auto sector grew 11%.
White-collar hiring grew marginally by 2% year-on-year in September, mainly driven by record growth in AI/ML roles, followed by the auto sector, a report said on Friday.
White-collar hiring remained largely steady in September, growing 2% year-on-year, with the Naukri JobSpeak Index reaching 3,053 compared to 3002 in the year-ago month, according to a report by Naukri.com, Info Edge's flagship brand.
The Naukri JobSpeak report is a monthly index that tracks trends in India's job market and hiring activity, based on new job postings (including free job listings) and recruiter searches on Naukri.com's platform.
The report revealed that Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) roles continued to record growth, rising 20% in September, while the Auto sector grew 11%.
BPO/ITES and GCC hiring grew 4% each during the month, the report added.
Among other key sectors, Insurance, Retail, Banking and Financial Services and Real Estate remained largely stable, while hiring declined across IT/Software Services (4%), Pharma/Biotech (4%), FMCG (4%) and Healthcare (3%).
Hospitality and Travel (11%) and Education (18%) recorded sharper declines, the report added.
Meanwhile, hiring remained largely stable at the entry and early-mid career levels, with fresher hiring witnessing an increase of 1% year-on-year and the 4-7 years experience band declining by 2%.
Demand continued to remain stronger for experienced professionals, growing 5% for 8-12 years, 7% for 13-16 years and 5% for over 16 years.
Among metros, Hyderabad recorded 9% year-on-year growth, followed by Chennai at 6%, and Bengaluru and Kolkata at 4% each.
While Pune remained stable, Delhi-NCR and Mumbai declined 6% each; hiring growth across emerging cities remained largely flat in September.
"September's numbers reflect a hiring market that remains steady, but more selective. While overall hiring was broadly stable, demand continued to move towards specialised skills, particularly AI, and more experienced professionals.
"The variation across sectors and cities also highlights that hiring is increasingly being driven by specific business and capability needs," Info Edge (India) Limited MD and CEO Hitesh Oberoi said.

articles.title: Frontline Education breach exposes school district employee data
articles.text:
Frontline Education is notifying school districts of a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in third-party software to gain unauthorized access to its systems and steal employee information, including Social Security numbers.
Frontline Education is an edtech company that provides administration and workforce management software and services used by school districts.
Last night, a reader shared a data breach notification with BleepingComputer that Frontline sent to an impacted school district, stating that attackers breached its environment through a vulnerability in a third-party application.
"On August 14, 2026, our security team identified a vulnerability in a third-party software product we use that allowed unauthorized access to a portion of the environment," the notification letter reads.
"We promptly investigated the issue with the assistance of an independent cybersecurity firm, remediated the vulnerability, engaged with law enforcement, and took steps to further reinforce the security of our systems."
The company has not disclosed which third-party application was involved or when the unauthorized access first occurred.
For the notification seen by BleepingComputer, our source said all employees at the district were impacted, with exposed information including Social Security numbers, email addresses, and physical addresses.
BleepingComputer contacted Frontline Education yesterday about the breach but did not receive a reply to our email.
However, school IT administrators reported on the K12SysAdmin subreddit that district officials had begun to receive similar notifications.
One administrator initially said their superintendent and business manager received the notification on October 1 from frontline@notifications.cyberscout.com, but Frontline support had not yet confirmed whether the message was legitimate.
However, other administrators later said they had independently confirmed the breach notifications were legitimate.
"Can confirm this is legitimate. We've had verbal contact with our Frontline rep on it," one administrator reported.
One administrator also shared a copy of a Frontline notification stating that 1,210 employees associated with their district were impacted and that Social Security numbers, email addresses, and addresses were also exposed.
Frontline says it will handle notifications to affected individuals on behalf of impacted school districts unless a district opts out by October 16.
Districts that want to opt out can do so through www.frontline-transunion.com or by calling 833-516-8792. If a district opts out, Frontline says it will not provide notification services or reimburse the district for the costs of issuing its own notices.
Impacted adults are being offered two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection through TransUnion, while minors will be offered cyber monitoring services.
The company says it will also handle required notifications to state attorneys general and cover costs associated with individual notifications and the identity protection services.
It is unclear how many school districts or individuals were affected.

articles.title: La Citroën 2CV électrique à 15 000 € arrive : voici les premières images du concept présenté à Paris — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pendant longtemps, Citroën s’est refusé à réinterpréter ses anciennes gloires : le passé n’avait droit qu’à un hangar poussiéreux.
Le succès monstre de la Renault 5 E-Tech a-t-il donné des idées aux dirigeants ? Toujours est-il que Citroën a confirmé le retour de la 2CV sous la forme d’une voiture électrique à 15 000 euros lors de la conférence FaSTLAne présentant la nouvelle stratégie de Stellantis.
    Pour aller plus loin
2CV électrique, partenariats chinois et marques délaissées : voici toutes les annonces de Stellantis pour remonter la pente
            
Une voiture extrêmement attendue, donc, sur laquelle Citroën compte bien communiquer. Première étape : un concept-car présenté au Mondial de l’Auto de Paris, qui ouvre dans quelques jours, et dont la campagne de teasers a débuté sur Instagram.
Une inspiration évidente
Le teaser aussi flou que sombre de la conférence nous avait mis la puce à l’oreille, les premières images ne font que confirmer : ce concept de Citroën 2CV électrique sera une réinterprétation fidèle de la plus célèbre des voitures françaises.
Les détails illustrés ne laissent aucune place au doute. Les phares arrondis et sortis de la carrosserie, le capot bombé et strié, le pavillon « parapluie » avec le clignotant en hauteur, les poignées de porte pivotables ou encore l’orange de la carrosserie, hommage à la 2CV Spot : les clins d’œil, à défaut d’être particulièrement subtils, font mouche.
Évidemment, le design et les détails seront contemporains. On peut par exemple découvrir des phares LED, tandis que les jantes prennent leurs aises (notons la jolie typographie Michelin des pneus).
Une voiture de série en 2028
Ce concept de 2CV électrique sera officiellement révélé le 11 octobre à 19h00 avant sa présentation au public le 12 octobre, à l’ouverture du Mondial de l’Auto à Paris – d’ici là, la campagne de teasers devrait suivre son cours.
Le mystère reste donc entier sur le design global du concept, de même que son habitacle ou d’éventuels détails techniques.
En tout cas, une chose est sûre : la voiture de série sortira en 2028, à un tarif démarrant sous les 15 000 euros. Il s’agit d’une des citadines électriques du projet E-Car de Stellantis, qui sera accompagnée d’un équivalent chez Fiat avant une troisième marque encore à déterminer.
Le positionnement exact de ces citadines électriques, il faut bien l’avouer, reste à déterminer. Stellantis espère beaucoup de la catégorie M1E en cours de discussion à la Commission européenne, visant les petites voitures électriques produites en Europe.
    Pour aller plus loin
« C’est un big deal » : le patron de Fiat nous parle de ses futures voitures électriques à 10 000 et 15 000 €
            
Il se pourrait également que Stellantis suive l’exemple du Dacia Hipster avec une homologation en tant que quadricycle lourd (catégorie L7e), débloquant un assouplissement des normes de sécurité en échange d’une vitesse limitée à 90 km/h.
Rendez-vous le 11 octobre pour avoir des premières pistes. Reste un doute : si Citroën nous fait trop saliver avec un concept alléchant mais techniquement irréalisable en série, n’ouvre-t-il pas la porte à une vague de déception des clients avec une voiture de série fatalement plus tiède ?

articles.title: 39 years in tech, one hard lesson: Lungi Sangqu on why buying software won't fix broken processes - TechCabal
articles.text:
Thirty-nine years ago, Lungi Sangqu wrote her first lines of code. Nearly four decades later—after shaping digital systems across 49 African countries in banking, rail, logistics, and higher education—her most profound lesson has nothing to do with software. For this week’s Coffee With…, PHATHISANI MOYO sits down with the founder and CEO of Africa Digital Success to discuss why millions in enterprise tech spending go to waste, why C-suites must stop delegating strategy solely to IT departments, and what these years in computing teach us about AI and the human element of work.
In 1987, Lungi Sangqu discovered computer science and became captivated by its capacity to solve complex problems at speed. At the time, computing remained a novelty to most people in her community, but for Sangqu, it provided a clear window into tomorrow.
“I knew that I was learning about the future,” she told TechCabal.
Nearly four decades later, as the founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Africa Digital Success, a pan-African digital transformation consultancy, Sangqu has spent her career helping institutions navigate that very future. Her work has spanned government, banking, education, logistics, and rail infrastructure across South Africa and the wider continent.
Yet her most profound insight has little to do with code or hardware. Technology can execute flawlessly according to specification and still fail the human beings expected to adopt it. The dividing line between success and failure, Sangqu has learnt, rests on leadership decisions, human-centric system design, and whether executives truly comprehend the problem they are attempting to solve.
A curiosity that began in Mthatha
Sangqu was raised in Mthatha, in South Africa’s Eastern Cape Province, attending Ross Primary School before completing her matriculation at Ngangelizwe High School. She subsequently pursued university studies in mathematics, chemistry, and computer science.
Computer science captured her imagination in 1987. Intrigued by the sheer speed with which algorithms could resolve complex calculations, she advanced through Computer Science III.
While her early technical grounding laid the foundation for her career, decades of practical application broadened her perspective on technology’s ultimate purpose.
“Mathematics taught me discipline; technology taught me possibility; working in institutions taught me that both must be placed in service of people,” she reflects.
Starting as a software programmer in the early 1990s, Sangqu developed a sharp eye for detail and a deep appreciation for the operational staff who keep systems running. As she transitioned into larger institutions, the core challenges grew increasingly complex.
The fundamental questions evolved beyond technical functionality. Instead, they centered on strategic alignment: Why did the organisation require this system? Who would operate it? What was the true cost-to-benefit ratio? Would it measurably improve service delivery?
“As I moved into larger organisations, I saw that the hardest technology problems often sat outside the code,” she explains.
Her career trajectory took her through high-stakes roles at the Public Service Commission, the Department of Social Development, the State Information Technology Agency (SITA), the South African Post Office, the South African Reserve Bank, DHL Express, the University of South Africa (UNISA), Walter Sisulu University, and Transnet Freight Rail.
At DHL, her operational scope spanned 49 African countries. Across these diverse environments, Sangqu observed a universal truth: organisations must always start with the problem, never the product.
“Every problem requires the right technology,” she emphasises.
Transforming South Africa’s largest distance learning institution
A defining example of this philosophy occurred during her tenure at UNISA, South Africa’s largest open-distance learning institution. Sangqu led initiatives to digitise student applications, registration, assignment submission, and grading workflows.
This was not merely an IT procurement exercise. The university had to re-engineer core processes, train administrative staff, and evaluate whether digital tools served the institution’s educational mandate. By August 2013, UNISA had successfully transitioned assignment marking fully online.
However, the transition highlighted crucial equity considerations. Students required compatible devices and reliable broadband. While digital workflows streamlined operations for urban learners, they created friction for rural students lacking internet access.
For Sangqu, this underscores why digital initiatives cannot be evaluated solely by launch milestones.
“A successful launch is only a milestone,” she notes. “The real test is whether the organisation can sustain the change and whether the people it serves experience a tangible improvement.”
Addressing the governance and leadership deficit
After decades within major public and private enterprises, Sangqu grew troubled by how institutions evaluated digital investments. Too often, executive boards celebrated the acquisition of expensive platforms rather than improvements in customer experience, staff productivity, or decision-making quality.
She frequently witnessed organisations pouring millions into software without establishing a clear link to operational efficiency or revenue growth. In many instances, technology was brought into executive discussions as an afterthought—long after business strategy had been set.
To bridge this gap, Sangqu founded Africa Digital Success. The consultancy provides executive-level advisory services, helping leadership teams navigate technology risk, upskill talent, and execute sustainable digital strategies.
“The core gap was this,” she states. “Organisations were measuring technology by the wrong metrics, counting the platforms they acquired rather than asking whether technology helped them serve customers and citizens better.”
The habits that hold organisations back
One of the most persistent problems, she says, is the belief that technology belongs to the information technology (IT) department and that other executives need not concern themselves with it.
That separation can leave technology teams responsible for decisions they cannot make alone. A new system may require changes to budgets, staffing, customer service or everyday working practices. Without support from senior leaders, even a well-designed project can struggle.
Other habits create similar problems. Some organisations treat technology mainly as a cost to be reduced. Others assume an expensive international product must be better than a locally developed alternative. Departments may also keep information to themselves, making it harder for colleagues to see the full picture.
Slow approval processes can push employees to find their own solutions. A team unable to get permission for a digital tool may buy software independently or store information outside approved systems. Although this may help solve an immediate problem, it can leave the organisation exposed to security risks and unable to manage its information properly.
“Shadow IT is a governance and trust problem,” Sangqu said.
Her answer is not simply to impose more rules. Leaders need to take responsibility for technology decisions, while making internal processes clear and practical enough for employees to follow.
She also wants organisations to assess local technology on its merits rather than dismissing it before testing it. Products should be judged on whether they are reliable, secure, affordable and suitable for the organisation’s needs, not on where they come from or how familiar the supplier’s name is.
When organisations work with local providers, they can also create opportunities for skills development and knowledge transfer. Buying a system should not leave an organisation permanently dependent on an outside supplier.
AI, youth talent, and building enduring workplaces
These governance principles have become urgent as artificial intelligence reshapes the workplace. Sangqu advises boards to define the specific operational problem before deploying AI, verify data integrity, and establish clear human oversight.
Furthermore, leaders must plan for workforce transitions when tasks are automated—re-skilling employees for higher-value roles rather than viewing automation solely through a cost-reduction lens.
She sees a similar mandate regarding young professionals entering the workforce. Many arrive with native digital literacy, only to be stifled by manual workflows and risk-averse managers who value physical presenteeism over output.
“We cannot ask young professionals to innovate while requiring them to spend their days repairing avoidable gaps in legacy systems,” she remarks.
While institutional history and senior mentorship remain vital, Sangqu stresses that knowledge exchange must be reciprocal. Established leaders must listen to younger staff who can spot operational inefficiencies.
From writing raw code in 1987 to advising enterprise boards today, Sangqu’s career reflects a singular conviction: digital progress is measured by what it enables human beings to achieve.
Through Africa Digital Success, her goal is to build self-sustaining institutional capacity across the continent.
“I want younger Africans to inherit workplaces where their ideas can seamlessly become meaningful, impactful work,” she reflects.
For a pioneer whose journey began with the promise of computer logic nearly 40 years ago, Sangqu’s ultimate focus remains squarely on the human beings behind the machine.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: El mítico bar de Madrid donde se rodó esa escena de 'La bola negra': café de pota y una familia al frente desde 1959
articles.text:
Durante una jornada, un pequeño comedor de La Latina se llenó de focos, cámaras y técnicos. Hubo que reorganizar las mesas y repetir la escena una y otra vez, y el problema fue una fabada: cada plano exigía que el plato mantuviera el mismo aspecto durante horas. Lo cuenta EPE de La Copita Asturiana, en la calle Tabernillas (Madrid), donde Los Javis (Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi) rodaron una escena clave de ‘La bola negra’, la película que arrasó en Cannes 2026 y se llevó el premio a Mejor dirección, ganó también el del público en el 74º Festival de San Sebastián y ya aspira al Oscar.
Eligieron este bar porque ya eran clientes. Cualquiera puede ir, claro.
Del vino en chato al café de pota. Cuando Mari y Pepe abrieron La Copita Asturiana, el 20 de mayo de 1959, el local ya llevaba más de medio siglo como despacho de vinos para el barrio: según la web del propio restaurante, funcionaba como tal desde 1904. Pepe lo conocía de antes, porque lo frecuentaba como cliente en los años cincuenta, y decía que lo trataba desde hacía más de seis décadas. Al hacerse cargo, les dijeron que a ver si tenían más suerte que los últimos dueños.
Las mesas eran de mármol, se tomaban chatos de vino y se picaban raciones sencillas: patatas de la fayona, lacón, manitas, callos, caldo gallego, escabeches. Algunos de esos platos todavía están en la carta. Poco a poco la cocina asturiana se impuso: fabada, fabes con almejas, verdinas, pote, cachopo, chosco de Tineo. Mari tenía 16 años y Pepe 27 cuando llegaron, tal y como indican desde El Economista. En 2018, su hija Olga dejó la economía para seguir con el negocio junto a su marido, José María. Mari, de 83 años, sigue pendiente de todo.
De raciones a fabadas. Fue Mari, siempre al frente de los fogones, quien fue incorporando las fabes con almejas y la fabada cuando los vecinos dejaron de ir a jugar la partida y empezaron a ir a comer. El boca a boca hizo el resto: hoy, cuenta la casa, reciben clientes de Francia, México, Estados Unidos e incluso Australia.
Además de la propia Mari también cocina la hija, y José María atiende la sala con ellas. Según cuentan, la fabada se hace a fuego lento desde las 8:30 de la mañana, sin ollas a presión. La faba viene de Barcia y el embutido, de Tineo. Tiene un Solete Repsol y el presentador Arturo Valls es habitual del local.
De película. No puedo hablar de la calidad de dicha fabada pero sí de cómo transcurre en la película de marras. Sin soltar mucho spoiler de la película, Alberto, un joven historiador, y su madre, Teresa, comen una fabada en un enorme bol de cristal y en un almuerzo tenso que acaba mal y pronto, con cerveza lanzada incluida. La revista Interiores la sitúa entre las secuencias más tensas del filme, porque deja al descubierto una relación complicada.
A Alberto lo interpreta Carlos González (‘Veneno’, ‘La vida breve’) y a Teresa, Lola Dueñas (‘La Mesías’, ‘Volver’). Comparten reparto con Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Penélope Cruz y la incombustible Glenn Close. El rodaje empezó en agosto de 2025 en el pueblo abandonado de Castil de Carrias (Burgos). Dos meses después, el equipo se trasladó a Madrid para las escenas finales, así que el día en La Copita fue probablemente en otoño.
UN VISTAZO A...
Querido y protegido. La fachada original está catalogada como "Elemento Protegido", y el mostrador de estaño, según esa guía, también. El Catálogo de Elementos Protegidos del Plan General incluye locales comerciales y regula qué se puede cambiar en ellos. Es una protección arquitectónica, lo que significa que no obliga a seguir con la actividad ni fija el alquiler. El ticket medio va de 30-40 euros a 40-50, según algunos medios. Abre solo a mediodía y en 2023 recibió un Premio Platino de Hostelería Madrid.
Zara: 160 servicios al día y 7.440 kilómetros. Al otro lado de este éxito, esta misma semana El País contaba que cierra Zara, el cubano de Chueca abierto cinco años después que La Copita, en 1964. Dos casas familiares con fundadores asturianos llamados Pepe: una sigue y la otra baja la persiana el sábado 17 de octubre a mediodía.
La historia de Zara es diferente, empieza en La Habana: Pepe salió de un pueblo asturiano a los 16 años en un barco de carga desde Gijón, un mes de viaje. Conoció a Inés en diciembre de 1957 en el Centro Asturiano de La Habana. En 1961 dejaron Cuba y en 1964 cogieron el traspaso de una cafetería madrileña que ya se llamaba Zara. Su dueño, zaragozano, se quedó sin dinero para completar el luminoso.
Y los platos cubanos entraron por casualidad: se los hacían para comer y los daban a probar. Así nacieron los menús del día y llegaron a dar hasta 160 servicios diarios. En 1978, la cafetería se hizo restaurante y se convirtió en punto de encuentro de la comunidad cubana en Madrid. Al menos el cierre no es por una mala noticia: en 2014 se mudaron a la calle Barbieri y ahora quieren descansar (ella quiere escribir y él, arquitecto, estudiar de nuevo).
Ambos negocios comparten lo esencial: familia, fundadores asturianos, comida casera y clientela fiel. Eso sí, si vas, te recomiendo hacer reserva: el local es pequeño y solo abre a mediodía.
