articles.title: Top 50: Europe's most influential AI leaders | EU-Startups
articles.text:
For a long time now it has been hard to escape the impact AI has been having on our daily personal and professional lives.
What may have started as a curiosity for many; generating an image, asking a chatbot a question or experimenting with a new productivity tool, has rapidly developed into a technology reshaping how companies operate, how research is conducted and how entire industries approach their future.
Europe has been an important part of that global development. Across the continent, researchers, founders and technology leaders are building everything from frontier models and AI agents to healthcare applications, infrastructure, cybersecurity tools and autonomous systems. At the same time, established European companies are incorporating AI into products and operations that already reach millions of people.
Behind those developments are individuals making decisions about what gets researched, built, funded and deployed.
Presented alphabetically, this list brings together 50 of Europe’s most influential AI leaders.
Alex Kendall – Wayve (UK)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Wayve, founded in 2017, who are developing end-to-end embodied-AI systems for automated driving. Kendall has built Wayve around an AI-first approach to driving, using learned models rather than relying primarily on hand-engineered rules.
Alexandre LeBrun – Nabla/Advanced Machine Intelligence (France)
CEO of Paris-based Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI), founded 2025 by Yann LeCun to develop world models for AI reasoning. LeBrun previously co-founded medical AI startup Nabla and Wit.ai, acquired by Facebook in 2015, spending over a decade building conversational and applied AI technologies.
Anastasia Georgievskaya – Haut.AI (Estonia)
Co-founder and CEO of Haut.AI, an Estonian computer-vision company founded in 2018 that uses AI to analyse skin and enable personalised skincare. With a background in bioengineering and biophysics, Georgievskaya has built the company around translating visual biomarkers into commercial AI applications.
Anders Hammarbäck – Redpine (Sweden)
Co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Redpine, founded in 2024 to provide AI companies and agents with licensed access to high-quality proprietary data. Hammarbäck is addressing one of the emerging constraints on AI development: access to reliable, specialised datasets beyond publicly available web content.
Angie Ma – Faculty (UK)
Co-founder of London-based Faculty, an applied-AI company founded in 2014 working with businesses and governments to develop and deploy artificial-intelligence systems. Ma has helped build Faculty while also contributing to discussions around AI adoption, skills and the development of the UK technology ecosystem.
Anton Osika – Lovable (Sweden)
Co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Lovable, an AI software creation platform founded in 2023 that enables users to build applications through natural-language instructions. Osika has turned the company into an example of how AI is changing the process of software creation.
Arthur Mensch – Mistral AI (France) 
Co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Mistral AI, one of Europe’s leading frontier-AI companies founded in 2023. A former Google DeepMind researcher, Mensch has positioned Mistral as a European alternative to US AI labs while expanding its models and enterprise products across international markets.
Carla Gómez Cano – THEKER (Spain)
CEO of Barcelona-based THEKER which she co-founded in 2022. Gómez Cano is building technology that combines AI, computer vision and robotics to automate complex physical tasks, positioning her work at the intersection of Europe’s emerging physical-AI and advanced-manufacturing sectors.
Charles Delingpole – ComplyAdvantage (UK)
Founder of London-based ComplyAdvantage, established in 2014 to use AI and data to tackle financial crime, sanctions and compliance risk. Delingpole built the company around machine-learning systems that help financial institutions screen customers and transactions.
Clément Delangue – Hugging Face (France/US)
Co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face, the French-founded AI company established in 2016 that has become a central platform in the global open-source AI ecosystem. Under Delangue, it has developed into a widely used hub for machine-learning models, datasets and tools used by researchers, developers and enterprises.
Dawid Kotur – Curvestone AI (UK)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Curvestone AI, founded in 2023 to develop reliable AI automation for regulated industries. Kotur is focused on deploying AI in compliance-intensive environments where auditability, security and dependable human oversight remain important constraints on automation. Read Dawid’s insights here.
Demis Hassabis – Google DeepMind (UK)
Chair of Google DeepMind, which he co-founded in 2010, is a London-based AI research laboratory behind advances including AlphaFold. Hassabis, a neuroscientist and AI researcher, was jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on protein structure prediction.
Dimitris Vassos – Omilia (Cyprus)
Co-founder and CEO of Omilia, the conversational‑AI company he co-founded in Athens in 2002. Vassos has spent more than two decades developing speech and natural‑language technologies, building Omilia around automated customer interactions and conversational AI systems for large enterprises.
Emanuela Girardi – Pop AI / ADRA (Italy)
Founder and CEO of Pop AI and President of ADRA – the European Association for AI, Data and Robotics. Girardi works across industry, research and EU strategy to accelerate AI adoption and connect companies, researchers and policymakers around Europe’s AI, data and robotics ecosystem.
Eno Thereska – Trent (UK)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Trent, a cybersecurity company founded in 2025 that develops protection for AI agents and autonomous workflows. Thereska is addressing security risks created as businesses give AI systems greater access to corporate software, infrastructure and sensitive data.
Fernando Oliver Jané – Mafer AI (Spain)
Co-founder and CEO of Barcelona-based Mafer AI, founded in 2025 to build an AI-native operating system for R&D teams in formulation industries. Jané applies AI to complex technical workflows in chemicals, food and beverage, cosmetics and personal care.
Frank Hutter – Prior Labs (Germany)
Co-founder and CEO of Prior Labs, a German frontier AI company founded in 2024 that develops foundation models for tabular data. A researcher in automated machine learning, Hutter is translating years of academic work into models designed to reason over the structured data underpinning businesses and scientific research.
Henna Virkkunen – European Commission (Finland/EU)
Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy. Virkkunen is responsible for the Digital and Frontier Technologies portfolio, including EU work on AI innovation, cloud, high-performance computing and quantum technologies
Henri Taskinen – Capalo AI (Finland)
Co-founder and CEO of Helsinki-based Capalo AI, founded in 2022 to apply AI to battery storage and electricity markets. Taskinen is using AI optimisation to operate virtual power plants and maximise the value of distributed energy assets within increasingly complex electricity grids.
Jarosław Kutylowski – DeepL (Germany)
Founder and CEO of Cologne-based DeepL, founded in 2017 and now one of Europe’s best-known language-AI companies. Kutylowski expanded the business from neural machine translation into AI writing and enterprise language tools, building a globally adopted product around specialised language models.
Joan Vendrell – NeuralTrust (Spain)
Co-founder and CEO of Barcelona-based NeuralTrust, founded in 2023 to develop security and governance infrastructure for generative AI and enterprise agents. Vendrell is focused on helping companies monitor, secure and control autonomous systems as AI gains access to increasingly sensitive corporate data and workflows.
Jonas Andrulis – Aleph Alpha (Germany)
Founder and CEO of Heidelberg-based Aleph Alpha, a sovereign AI company founded in 2019 that develops foundation models and enterprise AI infrastructure. Andrulis has made the company a prominent part of Europe’s effort to develop AI systems for governments and organisations operating in regulated environments.
Josh Payne – Nscale (UK)
Founder and CEO of Nscale, a British AI infrastructure company founded in 2024 that builds large-scale GPU compute and data-centre infrastructure. Payne is focused on the physical computing layer required to train and run increasingly demanding AI models at scale.
Karim Beguir – InstaDeep (UK/Tunisia)
Co-founder and CEO of InstaDeep, the AI systems company founded in 2014 and subsequently acquired by BioNTech in 2023. Beguir helped build the company into a developer of advanced machine-learning and decision-making systems with applications spanning biotechnology, logistics and other complex industrial problems.
Katerina Spranger – Oxford Heartbeat (UK)
Founder and CEO of Oxford Heartbeat, a medical-technology company founded in 2015 which uses AI to support the planning of cardiovascular procedures. An Oxford-trained biomedical engineer, Spranger has combined AI research with entrepreneurship to develop technology designed to help clinicians select and assess medical devices for individual patients.
Luc Julia – Renault Group (France)
Chief Scientific Officer at Renault Group, Julia is a French computer scientist and AI specialist whose career has spanned research and senior technology roles in Europe and the US. In his role at Renault Group, Julia advises on scientific and technology matters, including AI and mobility.
Lukas Saari – Tandem Health (Sweden)
Co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Tandem Health, founded in 2023 to develop an AI assistant and operating system for healthcare professionals. Saari is focused on reducing clinical administration and embedding language models into medical workflows while keeping clinicians at the centre of decision-making.
Mati Staniszewski – ElevenLabs (UK/Poland)
Co-founder and CEO of ElevenLabs, the British-Polish generative voice and audio AI company founded in 2022. Staniszewski has overseen its expansion from realistic text-to-speech into voice cloning, dubbing, multilingual audio and conversational AI applications.
Mikko Mäntylä – Realm (Finland)
Co-founder and CEO of Realm, a Finnish AI company founded in 2024 that develops autonomous agents for enterprise sales. Mäntylä is applying agentic systems to research and operational tasks surrounding complex B2B sales workflows.
Nathan Benaich – Air Street Capital (UK)
Founder and General Partner of London-based Air Street Capital, an AI-focused venture capital firm founded in 2020. Benaich combines investment in technical founders with his role as co-author of the widely followed State of AI Report.
Nicole Büttner – Merantix Momentum (Germany)
CEO of Merantix Momentum which she co-founded in 2018, a Berlin-based AI company that develops and deploys machine-learning solutions for organisations across different industries. Büttner combines AI entrepreneurship with broader work across Germany’s technology ecosystem.
Nigel Toon – Graphcore (UK)
Co-founder and former executive chair of Graphcore, a semiconductor company founded in 2016. Toon built one of Europe’s most ambitious AI-chip challengers, helping put specialised compute and semiconductor sovereignty on the European technology agenda.
Nuria Oliver – ELLIS Alicante Foundation (Spain)
Co-founder and Director of the ELLIS Alicante Foundation, a research institute founded in 2020 which focuses on human-centric AI, and Vice-President of the European Laboratory for Learning and Intelligent Systems.
Oana Jinga – Dexory (UK)
Co-founder and Chief Commercial & Product Officer of Dexory, a London-based robotics and warehouse-intelligence company founded in 2015 combining autonomous robots with real-time inventory data. Jinga has helped scale the company from its origins as BotsAndUs into an international Physical AI business. Watch Oana’s interview here.
Peter Sarlin – Silo AI / AMD (Finland)
Co-founder and former CEO of Helsinki-based Silo AI,  founded in 2017, which became one of Europe’s largest private AI laboratories before its acquisition by AMD in 2024. Sarlin has combined company-building, research and investment while remaining an advocate for strengthening Europe’s AI talent and infrastructure.
Renco Smeding – Ivy Interactive (Sweden)
Co-founder of Swedish startup Ivy Interactive, founded in 2024 to use generative AI to accelerate the development of bespoke internal software. Smeding is applying AI to the long tail of business applications that companies need but have traditionally been expensive and time-consuming to build.
Robin Rombach – Black Forest Labs (Germany)
Co-founder of Black Forest Labs, the generative-AI research company founded in 2024 behind the FLUX model family. Rombach was one of the key researchers behind latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion, work that has been central to the development of modern generative image AI.
Ruben Bryon – Verda (Finland)
Founder and CEO of Helsinki-based Verda, formerly DataCrunch, founded in 2020 and providing full-stack AI cloud and GPU infrastructure. Bryon is building European compute capacity for developers and enterprises as access to high-performance hardware becomes increasingly strategic to AI development.
Rudy Cohen – Inbolt (France)
Co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Inbolt, founded in 2019 to develop real-time vision and intelligence for industrial robots. Cohen is building hardware-agnostic AI technology that combines 3D vision with intelligent software, enabling robots to perceive changes in their environment and adapt their movements during manufacturing processes.
Saaras Mehan – Jack & Jill (UK)
Co-founder of London-based Jack & Jill, founded in 2024 to develop separate conversational AI agents for jobseekers and employers. Mehan is applying agentic AI to recruitment, automating parts of candidate discovery, matching and communication on both sides of the hiring market.
Tabitha Goldstaub – Lichen AI (UK)
CEO of Lichen AI which she co-founded in 2025, an AI company developing agentic technology for enterprise workflows. Goldstaub previously co-founded AI knowledge platform CognitionX and chaired the UK Government’s AI Council, combining AI entrepreneurship with work on adoption, governance and the development of the UK’s wider artificial-intelligence ecosystem.
Thomas Clozel – Owkin (France)
Co-founder and CEO of Paris-founded Owkin, established in 2016 to apply AI to biological and clinical data for drug discovery. A physician and former clinical haematologist, Clozel has built one of Europe’s prominent companies at the intersection of AI, biotechnology and precision medicine.
Tobias Haefele – Riplo (UK)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Riplo, founded in 2025 to build an agentic operating system for consulting and professional services. Haefele is applying AI agents to research, analysis and knowledge work in industries where substantial professional time remains tied to manual information processing.
Torsten Reil – Helsing (Germany)
Co-founder and co-CEO of Munich-based Helsing, founded in 2021 and focused on developing AI-powered software and autonomous systems for defence. Reil previously founded simulation and gaming technology company NaturalMotion before going on to build Helsing as a leading DefenceTech company.
Tyler Edwards – Overmind (UK)
Founder and CEO of London-based Overmind, founded in 2025 to develop security infrastructure for organisations deploying autonomous AI agents. A former MI5 officer, Edwards is applying experience from national-security environments to the challenge of supervising and controlling AI systems operating across enterprise software. Watch Tyler’s interview here.
Michael Lazarenko – Embedd (UK)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Embedd, founded in 2024 to develop software infrastructure for physical AI and semiconductor systems. Lazarenko is focused on reducing the complexity involved in connecting AI models and intelligent software with increasingly sophisticated physical hardware.
Valentin Neumann – Cortea (Germany)
Co-founder and CEO of Berlin-based Cortea, founded in 2024 to develop AI technology for auditing and professional services. Neumann is building systems designed to improve the quality and reliability of AI-assisted audit work in a field shaped by strict standards, documentation and regulatory requirements.
Vasilije Markovic – Cognee (Germany)
Founder and CEO of Cognee, a German AI infrastructure company founded in 2024 that develops memory technology for AI agents. Markovic is working on systems that allow autonomous agents to retain, structure and reason over context rather than treating every interaction as an isolated task.
Victor Riparbelli – Synthesia (UK/Denmark)
Co-founder and CEO of London-based Synthesia, founded in 2017 and now one of Europe’s prominent generative-AI companies. Riparbelli has built the company around AI-generated video, voices and digital presenters, turning synthetic media technology into an enterprise communications platform.
Yann LeCun – Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI) (France)
Founder and Executive Chairman of Paris-based Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI), founded in 2025 to develop world models intended to help AI systems understand physical environments, reason and plan beyond token-based language models. The Turing Award recipient and former Meta Chief AI Scientist is one of the world’s most influential AI researchers.

articles.title: Nuvio, la alternativa a Stremio que está ganando adeptos: qué es y cómo funciona
articles.text:
Stremio se ha convertido en la aplicación favorita de quienes buscan una alternativa ante tanta plataforma de streaming. Una manera diferente de disfrutar de contenidos por Internet sin tener que pelearte con suscripciones y catálogos que cambian sin darte cuenta. Pero todo va muy rápido en la red, y como Stremio es un proyecto de código abierto, era inevitable que, tarde o temprano, surgiera una alternativa a Stremio que quisiera mejorar lo inmejorable y responder a las demandas de quienes echan en falta algo en esta aplicación. Su nombre es Nuvio. Y aunque son muy parecidas, y ahí está la gracia, también son distintas entre sí.
De Stremio hemos hablado con anterioridad. Te hemos contado cómo instalar Stremio en tu televisor, en tu ordenador, cómo crear un servidor para compartir contenidos con tus otros dispositivos y las muchas ventajas de los addons de Stremio. Es más. Los addons o complementos son la razón de que esta aplicación sea hoy en día tan popular. En este sentido, Nuvio ha adoptado lo mejor de Stremio y ha incorporado alguna mejora allí donde Stremio se quedaba corta.
Pero vayamos por partes. Veamos en detalle qué es Nuvio exactamente, cómo funciona, sus parecidos y diferencias con Stremio, hasta qué punto ambas plataformas son compatibles y, finalmente, cómo empezar a disfrutar de Nuvio sin por ello dejar de utilizar Stremio. Con las dos podrás disfrutar de los mejores contenidos, sin salir de casa, y desde todos tus dispositivos conectados.
Qué es Nuvio
Nuvio es un cliente multimedia de código abierto que reproduce contenido audiovisual, como series o películas, a partir de los complementos que tú le instalas. Te sonará mucho porque Stremio es prácticamente eso. Tú le proporcionas tus fuentes de contenido y “Nuvio las convierte en una biblioteca con carátulas, valoraciones, subtítulos y tu posición guardada en cada pantalla”. De esta manera, puedes disfrutar de contenidos de aquí y de allá con la comodidad y experiencia visual de plataformas de streaming como Netflix o Prime Video.
Al ser un proyecto de código abierto, Nuvio se beneficia de otras herramientas multimedia con licencia similar. Por ejemplo, para reproducir todos los contenidos sin problemas en la mayoría de dispositivos, emplea aplicaciones como Media3 ExoPlayer y mpv, dos reproductores multimedia todoterreno compatibles con la mayoría de códecs de audio y video. Y que puedes usar en Android (ambos) o en Windows, macOS y Linux (el segundo).
Al igual que ocurre con Stremio, con Nuvio puedes organizar tu biblioteca de películas y series para estar siempre al día, descubrir nuevos títulos y reproducir contenido local o por streaming de distintas fuentes. Incluso puedes descargar ese contenido para cuando no tengas conexión. Entre otras cosas, Nuvio permite sincronizar tus visionados con Trakt, recibir avisos en tu teléfono cuando se estrenen nuevos capítulos de tus series favoritas, crear perfiles de usuario individuales y sincronizar toda esa información entre dispositivos.
En qué se parecen Stremio y Nuvio
Como habrás podido comprobar, Stremio y Nuvio tienen el mismo objetivo. Ser una alternativa ante el caos y la saturación de las plataformas de streaming. La oferta está tan fragmentada que cuesta encontrar contenido, organizar el visionado o encontrar algo entre tanto catálogo. Y gracias al uso de addons o complementos, puedes hacer de ambas aplicaciones un centro multimedia de lo más completo. En este sentido, aunque Nuvio y Stremio no comparten código, puedes instalar los addons de Stremio en Nuvio. Y los addons propios de Nuvio.
Otro parecido entre Nuvio y Stremio es que ambas aplicaciones están disponibles para la mayoría de dispositivos y sistemas operativos. Y al contar con sincronización de datos, esto te lo pone muy fácil para poder disfrutar de series, películas, documentales o dibujos animados estés donde estés: teléfono móvil, tableta, ordenador, televisor… Así no tendrás excusa para aprovechar el tiempo y ver una película o un capítulo de tus series en cualquier pantalla.
Diferencias entre Nuvio y Stremio
Si Stremio funciona tan bien y Nuvio se parece tanto, es obvio plantearte la siguiente pregunta: ¿por qué debería probar Nuvio? Además, Stremio es un proyecto más maduro, que lleva más tiempo entre nosotros. Sin embargo, Nuvio no quiere ser una simple alternativa a Stremio. Para empezar, su sistema de sincronización de datos es más completa. Y no tiene límite en la cantidad de perfiles a crear.
En segundo lugar, integra más servicios para que la experiencia sea más agradable. Además de Trakt y SIMKL, para saber qué contenidos has visto ya, importa metadatos y contenidos relacionados, como descripciones, fichas técnicas o tráilers, vía IntroDB, MDBList y The Movie DB. En este sentido, Stremio es más simple. Aunque es probable que encuentres addons puedas obtener funciones parecidas.
Dispositivos compatibles con Nuvio
Un motivo de peso para elegir entre Stremio y Nuvio es que puedas usarlo en tus dispositivos favoritos. Y ahí Stremio tiene las de ganar porque lleva más tiempo y ha tenido que sortear muchos impedimentos para estar ahí. Stremio está disponible para Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, Android TV, Fire TV, Apple TV, iOS/iPadOS, la mayoría de televisores inteligentes (Samsung, LG, Sony, Philips, Hisense) e incluso Steam Deck, Raspberry Pi, dispositivos NAS y Meta Quest. Y, por descontado, tiene versión Web.
Por su parte, Nuvio tiene aplicaciones para Windows, macOS, Linux, Android TV, Tizen (televisores Samsung), webOS (televisores LG) y Android. Y una versión Web. De momento, el ecosistema Apple se le resiste. Precisamente, Stremio ha tenido que batallar para lograr que su aplicación estuviera disponible en iOS/iPadOS/tvOS por las limitaciones de estas plataformas para aplicaciones como Nuvio y Stremio. Y, aún así, es necesario crear un servidor. Así que esta alternativa a Stremio tiene todavía mucho camino por recorrer.
Cómo empezar a usar Nuvio
La puesta en marcha de Nuvio es muy similar a la de Stremio. Sin entrar en detalles, y aunque hay ligeras diferencias entre plataformas y sistemas operativos, el proceso se podría resumir con los siguientes pasos:
- Instala Nuvio en tu dispositivo.
- Según la plataforma, hay instalador descargable o app vía tienda.
- Una vez instalado, abre la app.
- La primera vez, tendrás que crear una cuenta.
- Y, aunque es opcional, es recomendable activar la sincronización.
- Tercer gran paso, añadir addons.
- Se instalan de forma muy parecida a Stremio, como vimos aquí.
- Por comodidad, utiliza PC o Mac, ya que algunos addons se configuran desde una web.
- Cuando acabes, paséate por los ajustes de la aplicación.
- Allí podrás personalizar la interfaz, la reproducción de contenido…
- Y crear más perfiles.
- Y, para terminar, ya puedes explorar los catálogos incorporados vía addons.
Para terminar, si tienes cualquier duda sobre Nuvio, échale un vistazo a su página de preguntas más frecuentes. También puedes consultar su documentación oficial, aunque es algo técnica. Y, como vimos al principio, aunque es una seria alternativa a Stremio, puedes usar ambas aplicaciones por separado.

articles.title: Aplicaciones de seguimiento del ciclo menstrual conllevan riesgos para la salud de usuarias, según estudio
articles.text:
Alrededor de 50 millones de personas en el mundo utilizan aplicaciones para registrar su ciclo menstrual, los síntomas físicos y mentales asociados, la fertilidad y el embarazo. Sin embargo, un nuevo análisis publicado el miércoles en la revista médica revisada por pares ‘The BMJ’ sostiene que los riesgos vinculados a estas aplicaciones y otras herramientas digitales de seguimiento del ciclo, parte del mercado conocido como femtech, superan sus beneficios.
Los autores del artículo señalan que estos riesgos se extienden a las herramientas digitales que promueven el “cycle syncing”, práctica que consiste en basar la alimentación, el ejercicio y otros hábitos de vida en las distintas fases del ciclo menstrual.
“Esperamos que la gente entienda que muchas de las afirmaciones llamativas sobre el seguimiento y la sincronización del ciclo que circulan en redes sociales o en espacios de fitness y bienestar no están respaldadas por pruebas científicas”, declaró Katharine Lee, una de las autoras del artículo y profesora asistente del Departamento de Antropología de la Universidad de Tulane, en un correo electrónico a CNET.
Las estimaciones de ovulación carecen de precisión
Con base en varios estudios, el análisis afirma que la investigación en ciencias del deporte no permite generalizar cómo las distintas fases del ciclo menstrual afectan la salud. Estas correlaciones varían de forma individual. Lo mismo ocurre con las investigaciones sobre si la dieta puede reducir los síntomas del ciclo o mejorar el rendimiento, que en general resultan poco concluyentes o especulativas.
Incluso si estas conexiones existieran, el artículo sostiene que las herramientas digitales de seguimiento no podrían predecirlas. Las aplicaciones suelen basarse en la fecha de sangrado que reporta la propia usuaria para estimar la ovulación, la ventana fértil y las futuras fases del ciclo. Sin una medición real de las hormonas, estas estimaciones pueden resultar imprecisas, en particular porque tanto las hormonas como la ovulación fluctúan.
Los rastreadores digitales del ciclo menstrual tampoco pueden diagnosticar trastornos menstruales ni identificar las causas de los períodos dolorosos.
“Deberían trabajar con profesionales de la salud de confianza si tienen inquietudes, y sí, sé que a muchas personas les cuesta que sus médicos las escuchen sobre sus períodos”, afirmó Lee. “La gente puede querer registrar su ciclo por distintas razones, pero muchas aplicaciones de seguimiento digital no son más sofisticadas que contar y promediar datos”.
Al depender de estas aplicaciones, existe el riesgo de que las usuarias minimicen problemas de salud al atribuirlos simplemente a efectos del ciclo, o que dejen de lado las recomendaciones establecidas sobre dieta, ejercicio y sueño en nombre de la sincronización del ciclo.
La privacidad de los datos, otro punto de riesgo
A esto se suma el problema de la privacidad: algunas aplicaciones permiten el rastreo por parte de terceros, no publican informes de transparencia, no facilitan la eliminación directa de los datos y no utilizan almacenamiento local, lo que facilita la venta de información, su intercambio con terceros o su exposición ante filtraciones de datos. Esta situación resulta especialmente peligrosa en regiones donde el aborto está penalizado o donde existe mayor discriminación de género o sexo.
El análisis no menciona aplicaciones o herramientas específicas, aunque Lee indicó que varias de las referencias citadas se centran en las políticas o el funcionamiento de aplicaciones puntuales.
Pese a ser utilizadas y promocionadas ante millones de personas, el artículo sostiene que faltan pruebas que respalden la capacidad de estas herramientas para ayudar a gestionar el ciclo menstrual y la salud general.
Estas aplicaciones tampoco representan una solución a las desigualdades de género en el ámbito sanitario ni en la sociedad en su conjunto. Según el análisis, en cambio, ponen en riesgo la salud y la privacidad de las personas mientras les hacen perder tiempo y agravan las desigualdades existentes en el acceso a la seguridad, el descanso, la nutrición, la atención médica y los insumos menstruales.
El punto resulta especialmente relevante si se considera que muchas aplicaciones de seguimiento del ciclo utilizan en su publicidad el lenguaje del empoderamiento femenino.
Qué método de seguimiento recomiendan los expertos
No existe una única manera óptima de registrar el ciclo menstrual, ya que los métodos deberían adaptarse a las necesidades individuales.
Según Lee, quien busca información sobre fertilidad debería registrar signos de ovulación, como la temperatura basal corporal, la consistencia del moco cervical y los niveles de la hormona luteinizante.
En cambio, al gestionar condiciones de salud como la endometriosis, las migrañas o el trastorno disfórico premenstrual, que pueden variar con el ciclo, monitorear los síntomas asociados y predecir la próxima fecha estimada de sangrado puede resultar más relevante que concentrarse en la ovulación.
“La mayoría de las aplicaciones no pueden detectar la ovulación ni determinar en qué fase se encuentra alguien solo a partir del sangrado”, explicó Lee. “Incluso si estas aplicaciones simples pudieran detectar la ovulación y la fase del ciclo, no existen tendencias generalizables sobre lo que las personas experimentan”.
Quienes decidan registrar su ciclo mediante una aplicación deberían revisar previamente su política de privacidad.

articles.title: Istio 1.31 Adds Agentgateway Waypoints and Moves Release Artifacts off Google Cloud
articles.text:
Istio 1.31, released on 31 August, lets teams run agentgateway as a Layer 7 waypoint proxy in an ambient mesh, using the new istio-agentgateway-waypoint GatewayClass.
The same release stops publishing container images and Helm charts to Google Cloud. Teams still using gcr.io/istio-release, registry.istio.io, or the Google-hosted Helm repository should migrate before the next scheduled outage test on 13 October, ahead of their retirement in December. Istio 1.31.0 is supported on Kubernetes 1.32 to 1.36.
The waypoint support builds on the experimental gateway-only integration added in 1.30. Agentgateway is a Rust data plane built for agent traffic, donated by Solo.io to the Linux Foundation, and it handles protocols such as the Model Context Protocol alongside ordinary HTTP. Istio 1.31 also fixes ListenerSet handling and mTLS connectivity for agentgateway backends. Traffic shifting between waypoints is alpha, and the maintainers warn that the labels, annotations, and behaviour may change.
That shifting mechanism is new too. A service or namespace can name a canary alongside its primary waypoint through the use-waypoint-canary label, then send a configurable share of new in-mesh connections to the canary using the use-waypoint-canary-weight annotation, with no client-side changes. Established connections are not moved, so long-lived connections can delay the observed traffic split.
Istio 1.31.1, released on 21 September, fixes an issue where agentgateway waypoints referenced only as canaries were not programmed with the routes and policies of the services referencing them, causing shifted connections to be rejected. The patch also includes security fixes and corrects ALLOW_ANY_DYNAMIC_DNS forwarding in IPv6-only clusters.
Two traffic management additions stand out for large meshes. A new zoneAwareLbSetting field on DestinationRule and MeshConfig lets Envoy route to endpoints in the downstream proxy's own availability zone and spill over only when local capacity runs out, which Envoy decides automatically rather than through the static percentages localityLbSetting requires. The ALLOW_ANY_DYNAMIC_DNS outbound mode resolves hostnames from the HTTP Host header at request time, removing the need to write a ServiceEntry for every external destination.
On security, a fips-140-3 value for the COMPLIANCE_POLICY environment variable restricts TLS to version 1.2 or later, FIPS-compliant cypher suites and P-256 and P-384 curves. The change notes specify that Go components must be built with Go 1.24 or later using GOFIPS140=v1.0.0 or a later validated version; setting the runtime policy alone is insufficient. New trustDomains and notTrustDomains fields on AuthorizationPolicy match or exclude requests by the trust domain taken from the peer certificate.
The hosting change requires action from teams using the existing repositories. Writing on the Istio blog on 21 August, Steven Jin of Microsoft and Keith Mattix of Solo.io said "this year, Istio is migrating all of our infrastructure from Google Cloud Platform to Amazon Web Services due to changes in our funding model". The next scheduled scream test will disable the old endpoints on 13 October from 15:00 to 18:00 UTC; the final test runs from 8 December at 15:00 UTC to 9 December at 15:00 UTC. Teams verifying image signatures also need to account for key rotation: the migration guidance lists istio-key.pub for 1.31.0 and istio-key-v2.pub for 1.31.1 onwards. Asked on the tracking GitHub issue why the project chose Docker Hub over GHCR, Jin replied that "GHCR has some undocumented limits" and added, "I think we would easily blow past those given our current usage".

articles.title: Buying an RTX 5090 from Micro Center now means signing a form promising it won't leave the US
articles.text:
WTF?! It seems that if you have the money to buy a pre-built RTX 5090 PC from Micro Center, and there's one in stock, you'll also have to sign a declaration promising not to export the flagship graphics card. It's unclear exactly how enforceable this form is, though, and whether it would actually stop people who are selling the chips to China and elsewhere.
Redditor Krothic writes that they recently bought a PowerSpec Ai90 prebuilt PC packing an RTX 5090. The store manager informed them that buying the PC required that they fill in a form and have their drivers license scanned, connecting their name to their purchase.
After the section requiring details such as name, photo ID, and phone number, the form states that the person must be buying the PC for their own personal or business use in the US, "or I have accurately identified the actual end user above."
The next point specifies that the product will remain in the United States, and will not be exported, reexported, transferred, resold, supplied, or anything else that causes the PC to leave the US to any destination, for any reason.
These days, getting hold of an RTX 5090 usually means handing over more than $7,000, with at least one special edition model priced at $11,229. In many cases, it's cheaper to buy an entire pre-built PC featuring the GPU than to buy the card individually – and you obviously get all the other components as part of the price.
With its 32GB of VRAM, the RTX 5090 is considered as much of an AI-focused card as a gaming one, if not more so. As such, the standard RTX 5090 is restricted from export to mainland China under US export controls; Nvidia made separate 5090 D and 5090 D V2 versions for the Chinese market.
The Micro Center manager said the process had been in place for the past two days. There are certainly a lot of questions surrounding it. What if the buyer decides to sell the system or its GPU second-hand years later and that person then sells it overseas? What if the system is stolen and ends up abroad?
One comment on the thread also claims that Micro Center also won't sell an RTX 5090 to a customer if they've ever bought one in the past. Another user said the same thing happened to them.
Ultimately, this all feels like another reason why people aren't going to want to buy an RTX 5090, or a system containing one, right now. And, once again, it's AI's fault.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV is not a fan of AI-generated art | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Critics of AI-generated art have a powerful new ally: His Holiness the Bishop of Rome (Episcopus Romanus), Primate of Italy (Primatus Italiae), and Supreme Pontiff of the Universal Church (Summus Pontifex Ecclesiae Universalis).
In a post on X Friday morning, Pope Leo XIV detailed the spiritual difference between human-generated art and art that is generated by machines, as part of a call to preserve human art from the encroachment of AI.
“In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce,” the Servus Servorum Dei wrote. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”
Pope Leo XIV gave a more detailed statement on AI in an encyclical letter in May, which emphasized the importance of human dignity in a world of increasing automation.
But that hasn’t stopped AI companies from lobbying the supreme pontiff. According to a recent New York Times report, Anthropic has actively lobbied the Vatican to reconsider its position on non-human consciousness — apparently finding little success.

articles.title: Warlock ransomware breach SharePoint in water, telecom operator attacks
articles.text:
The China-linked ransomware group Warlock targeted a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body, and a university by exploiting SharePoint vulnerabilities to gain initial access.
Over the past two months, the threat actor appears to have focused on countries speaking Portuguese and Spanish across Europe, Africa, and Latin America.
The gang emerged in June 2025 and gained notoriety a month later after exploiting a chain of zero-day vulnerabilities in Microsoft SharePoint known as ToolShell (CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770, and CVE-2025-53771).
By August, Microsoft observed state-backed hacking groups Linen Typhoon and Violet Typhoon using ToolShell exploits in attacks, along with a ransomware threat actor the company tracks as Storm-2603.
EDR killer deployed to 40 hosts
Cybersecurity company Symantec identifies the same actor as Longlegs and attributes the development of the Warlock ransomware to the group.
According to the researchers, in one intrusion that started on July 22, the threat actor deployed a tool that disabled protection software on “at least 40 hosts within about two hours.” The attacker then launched Warlock ransomware on at least 33 hosts.
After gaining access, typically by exploiting vulnerabilities in on-premises SharePoint deployments, the attacker drops a web shell designed to function across multiple SharePoint versions.
Symantec and Carbon Black researchers say that in some attacks attributed to Longlegs, an AV/EDR-killing tool was deployed via the bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) technique using a signed K7RKScan driver vulnerable to CVE-2025-1055.
Analysis of the intrusion on July 22 revealed that two days after gaining initial access, the threat actor engaged in reconnaissance activity and deleted what seemed like staging artifacts.
Using VS Code's tunneling capability
The ransomware payload was staged in the domain’s SYSVOL share, a location that stores public files and is replicated across every domain controller.
This is “a known method of pushing a payload out for execution by a logon script or Group Policy object across an entire network at once, rather than one host at a time,” the researchers say.
During the attack, the main executable file for Visual Studio Code Insiders was installed as a service to enable connecting remotely to compromised machines using VS Code's built-in tunneling capability.
On one of the systems, the researchers found the open-source penetration testing framework NetExec, which helped the attacker with Active Directory enumeration, credential spraying, and remote command execution.
The final stage of the attack occurred on July 31st, after deploying the AV/EDR killer, with Warlock ransomware “appearing almost as soon as protection was disabled on each host.”
The researchers warn that ToolShell and other SharePoint vulnerabilities remain viable initial access vectors, more than a year after Warlock first emerged exploiting SharePoint flaws.
The report from the Symantec and Carbon Black threat hunters includes a set of indicators of compromise for files and infrastructure used in the attacks.

articles.title: Tesla vend plus de voitures que prévu, mais BYD creuse l’écart sur l’électrique - Numerama
articles.text:
Les publications trimestrielles de Tesla sont toujours un exercice d’équilibriste pour la marque. Après un début d’année plus chaotique que prévu, notamment à cause de la demande en Chine et aux États-Unis, le constructeur américain devait rassurer la Bourse avant sa conférence des résultats financiers prévue le 21 octobre.
En affichant 486 532 livraisons entre juillet et septembre 2026 dans son communiqué de presse du 2 octobre, Tesla fait mieux que le consensus établi par Wall Street autour de 462 000 unités. Tout n’est pas rose pour autant. Tesla ne peut plus clamer être le leader des véhicules électriques dans le monde.
De bons résultats malgré tout
Après un passage à vide au moment du renouvellement de son best-seller, Tesla affiche de nouveau de bons résultats. Le constructeur a livré 486 532 véhicules au troisième trimestre 2026. C’est 5,3 % de plus que les estimations des analystes compilées par le groupe.
En revanche, c’est 2,1 % de moins que le record établi un an plus tôt par la marque, justement quand les livraisons de son Model Y renouvelé ont tenté de faire oublier la traversée du désert des trimestres précédents. Le constructeur a livré 22 141 véhicules de plus qu’il n’en a produit, signe que les ventes se portent globalement bien malgré une concurrence de plus en plus rude.
Sans surprise, les Model 3 et Model Y ont représenté plus de 98 % de ses volumes. Tesla ayant fait sortir les derniers exemplaires de Model S et Model X au cours de cette période, la ligne « autres modèles » représente désormais essentiellement les Cybertruck et les premiers Tesla Semi. Avec 8 295 livraisons (pour 7 004 véhicules produits), cette ligne est pour le moment celle des flops de Tesla. Nous ne savons pas encore si les Cybercab seront intégrés à cette catégorie, et dans ce cas-là, la production des robotaxis de Tesla pourrait cacher le camouflet du Cybertruck.
La vraie satisfaction du trimestre vient de la division énergie. Avec 13,7 GWh de capacité de stockage déployée (Megapack et Powerwall), Tesla valide la montée en puissance de sa division réseau, même si le rythme reste légèrement sous les projections les plus optimistes des marchés pour tenir les objectifs annuels.
BYD ne laisse plus Tesla briller
Si Wall Street salue la capacité de Tesla à dépasser des attentes qui avaient été révisées à la baisse, la comparaison avec l’Asie modère l’excitation autour de ce résultat. Sur le marché chinois comme à l’exportation, le géant BYD continue d’afficher des volumes supérieurs à l’américain sur ses seuls véhicules électriques (donc sans s’appuyer sur les hybrides rechargeables).
Selon CNevpost, sur le seul mois de septembre 2026, BYD a frôlé la barre des 273 000 voitures 100 % électriques immatriculées. Sur le trimestre entier, BYD enregistre 762 478 véhicules électriques à batterie (VEB) de tourisme au troisième trimestre. En multipliant les lancements de gammes et en consolidant son intégration verticale sur les batteries, BYD relègue le rebond de Tesla au rang de simple résistance tactique.
BYD domine en Chine et sur de nouveaux marchés comme en Amérique latine, pendant que Tesla voit surtout ses résultats augmenter sur le marché européen, notamment porté par la hausse des prix des carburants. Il va être intéressant d’observer comment Elon Musk va défendre ce bilan lors des résultats financiers du 21 octobre. Le sujet des véhicules particuliers va certainement être éclipsé pour mettre l’accent sur les robotaxis.

articles.title: Continuous Health Monitoring Drives Integrated Wearable System Design - EE Times
articles.text:
The smaller a wearable electronics gadget gets, the more it has to do. A device that once tracked steps and heart rate now has to continuously capture physiological signals while making room for more sensors, optics, processing, and power management. That is pushing wearable designers to treat the optical, mechanical, sensing, and power domains as a connected system, rather than designing each function separately.
“We are seeing a lot of integration happening in devices,” said Praveen Jose, senior technical leader, field applications, at Analog Devices India, during a press briefing organized by the company. “Your devices become smaller and smaller, but the quality of the devices or the quality of the performance is increasing.”
Jose said the challenge is how to accommodate more functions within a small device and make it a single-body solution.
Sensio, an Indian startup developing smart rings, smart bands, and patches, focuses on wellness and health and claims its wearables collect heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, and activity data.
At the press briefing, Venkatesh Vadde, co-founder and CEO of Sensio, described how electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) can be used to estimate blood pressure continuously without a cuff, although he noted that the approach does not provide absolute blood pressure.
He said the startup works on embedding sensors in wearable devices, placing them at the right point, optimizing the signal, and using algorithms to interpret raw physiological signals.
That puts the optical path, sensor position, and physical construction of the wearable closer to the semiconductor design problem. Vadde said Sensio works with ADI sensors and other components and optimizes sensor placement, housing, and optics as part of the wearable design.
Identifying the problems
Jose said that optical sensing is challenging because the required physiological signal is embedded in noise. The sensing system needs to capture the required signal in the presence of noise before the data can be processed by algorithms or AI.
“In that particular scenario, you need to have a very good device which can actually sense the data in the presence of noise,” he said. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data.”
For a wearable designer, that means the optical assembly, sensor position, and mechanical construction can affect the quality of the electrical signal coming from the sensor. Vadde highlighted how closely the mechanical and optical aspects of the wearable are linked to PPG performance. The placement of the optical assembly relative to the skin affects the signal.
“Even a fraction of a millimeter lift-off of the optical assembly from the skin impacts PPG,” Vadde said.
The enclosure, housing, skin contact, optical assembly, and sensor placement therefore all have a bearing on the signal ultimately processed by the device.
For a ring, this becomes particularly important because the device has to maintain consistent contact with the skin while remaining small enough to be worn continuously, including during sleep.
The same system-level problem appears when the wearer moves. Vadde said motion artefacts, power consumption, and signal quality are real design challenges in wearable devices. The optics, mechanics, and housing have to be considered together.
This brings an accelerometer or inertial measurement unit (IMU) into the physiological sensing chain. In a consumer wearable, an accelerometer can be used to determine activity or movement. In a health-monitoring wearable, motion information can also help identify periods when another physiological measurement may be affected by motion artefacts.
Vadde said an IMU can be used to screen motion artefacts so that the system accepts higher-quality physiological data.
Jose described motion and activity detection as one of the functions being integrated into wearable platforms. “When we have something that we want to monitor, what we want to have is the motion to be sensed,” he said.
The signal quality can also affect power consumption. Vadde pointed to automatic gain control (AGC) as an example. When optical coupling or motion affects the quality of the signal, the system can increase the gain to recover the required signal. Depending on the implementation, that can also affect power consumption.
This creates a chain of interdependent design decisions—optical and mechanical design affect signal quality; signal quality affects analog processing and gain; processing affects power consumption; and power consumption affects battery life.
The power architecture also has to account for sensing frequency, processing, connectivity, and periods when the device does not need to operate at full activity. “Sometimes what happens is, when a person is taking rest, and we know that during different conditions more power is needed by the product, we will go into sleep mode or deep sleep mode, and the effect is to retain the battery power,” Jose said.
Connectivity is another consideration. Jose described the requirement as low-power to medium-power connectivity for continuous monitoring applications.
The frequency at which measurements are taken also affects battery life. Vadde said the required frequency of vital-sign measurements depends on the patient and the context. Taking measurements less frequently can extend battery life, while storing and synchronizing data rather than continuously transmitting it can also affect power consumption.
Combining sensing and power functions
The system-level problem is also shaping the way ADI approaches wearable customers. Vivek Tyagi, managing director, sales and country leader, at Analog Devices India, said the company sees two distinct types of customers: those with the capability to integrate optical components and those that require an easier-to-integrate approach.
Tyagi said the company has developed two types of solutions: sensor-hub devices that are easier for customers to use, and standalone solutions that he said can provide higher accuracy but require customers to have greater precision in integrating the optics, LEDs, and other elements.
ADI is also working on integrating sensing, power management, charging, and battery management functions. The company is also working on low-power solutions for applications such as continuous glucose monitoring. With ADI’s work on energy harvesting, mechanical movement or a temperature gradient can be converted into a small amount of electrical power that can be used to charge the device and extend battery life.
Jose said ADI’s solutions cover PPG, temperature sensing, ECG, and accelerometers, alongside power and connectivity functions.
For ring applications, Jose referred to Analog Devices MAX86178, while Vikash Singh, product application staff engineer, Healthcare Marketing and Applications, at Analog Devices India, described the MAX86184 as a small-form-factor PPG analog front end (AFE) designed for ring applications, with support for up to 14 LEDs and four photodiodes and dual-channel capability.
The MAX86178 is a more broadly integrated vital-sign analog front end (AFE) that combines PPG, ECG, and BioZ functions; its PPG section supports up to six LEDs and four photodiode inputs.
ADI is trying to bring more of the functions required by the wearable into fewer devices, while leaving customers with different levels of integration depending on their optical and system-design capabilities.
Tyagi said ADI is engaging customers earlier in their product roadmaps to understand what they want to build two or three years ahead and then co-create solutions.
“Then engage with a strategic partnership early on in their design journey, so that we can co-create a solution,” he said.
The sensing chain becomes the design problem
The trend toward continuous health monitoring is changing what has to be considered when designing a wearable.
Temperature sensors have to fit within small form factors while maintaining accuracy. Optical sensors have to extract physiological signals from noisy environments. Mechanical construction and sensor placement affect optical coupling. Motion information can be used to identify artefacts. Analog processing can compensate for weak signals but may affect power consumption. Connectivity has to transmit or synchronize the resulting data without exhausting the battery.
Jose said the quality of the sensed data is central to continuous monitoring. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data,” he said.
For wearable designers, the implication is that the sensing problem extends beyond an individual sensor. Optical and mechanical design, motion sensing, analog processing, algorithms, connectivity, and power all affect how a wearable collects and handles physiological data over time.
As wearables move from tracking activity toward continuous health monitoring, the engineering challenge is increasingly how these functions work together inside a device with very little room for error and physical space.

articles.title: 3D movies are finally worth watching
articles.text:
Why am I suddenly buying up every 3D Blu-ray I can find after 3D became one of the biggest tech flops of all time?
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
The technology’s finally ready for 3D movies to shine, more than 15 years since James Cameron’s Avatar wowed me on the big screen and went on to become the highest-grossing film worldwide. Video glasses are giving me the experience I’ve always desired.
I’ve always loved 3D movies, but viewing them was awkward. Walking into a movie theater with a pair of polarized glasses, I would only get half the resolution and roughly half the brightness, since those glasses had to split one reflected image between my two eyes. Almost every 3D technology cuts something you care about in half, whether it’s resolution (see also: Nintendo 3DS) or the refresh rate and flicker you get with active shutter glasses.
But what if you had a full screen for each eye? That’s what video glasses can provide.
Last year, I began testing a pair of Xreal One Pro glasses, which primarily give you a gigantic flat screen, like a private theater, for whatever you plug in. But that screen doesn’t technically need to stay flat. If you press and hold the right button, Xreal can give you independent left and right views for side-by-side (SBS 3D) content. With proper content, you get a full 1080p view for each eye.
There are SBS 3D toggles in popular video player apps for VR headsets like the Meta Quest and Steam Frame, too — and the Apple Vision Pro and upcoming Meta VR Glasses let you natively stream 3D films.
They’re breathtaking.
The water in Moana, a glass-covered clock in Zootopia 2, the helmets in Gravity, suiting up in giant robots in Pacific Rim, lightcycles in Tron: Legacy, comic book panels coming to life in Into the Spider-Verse — there’s just so much more depth to see.
When the ocean parts to let Moana through, it no longer feels like looking at a flat wall of water. It’s a living chunk of ocean with life swimming inside. The Lego Movie went from “wow those are some realistic-looking CG Lego bricks on a flat screen” to “I just got teleported into an entire Lego diorama.” In Avatar, the holographic displays in the ops room are mind-blowing. Even the flat rectangular monitors have 3D layers within.
Cockpits and helmets and Tron: Legacy lightcycles and Mad Max: Fury Road’s convoy of battling vehicles — anything with transparent glass is a treat. There’s distinct detail on the faces inside the glass, the structures outside, beads of water or scratches on the glass itself, even reflections of the outside world, depending on the film.
Billie Eilish’s new concert film, shot by James Cameron with 16 twin cameras including four remote-controlled AGITO camera rigs, looked incredible in the Meta VR Glasses during a brief demo. He got up close and personal with the concert, like few VR concert recordings do. In a demo with the Google / Xreal Aura, I watched a tiny bit of the interactive nature documentary Galapagos: The Last Eden and was entranced by the gorgeous baby seals, the grains of sand in their shiny fur, the fuzzy depth of the hair on their skin.
Regardless of the hardware, it almost feels like I can reach out and touch a character’s face in 3D, feel their emotions and wrinkles and scars more vividly, once they have depth.
Or, in the case of Werner Herzog’s cult-classic 3D documentary Cave of Forgotten Dreams, I could appreciate how the world’s oldest surviving art isn’t flat — the 32,000-year-old cave paintings took form thanks to their three-dimensional canvas. “A bulging rock is now a bulging neck of a bison that attacks you,” Herzog explained to us earlier this year.
When I fired up Gravity for what I thought would be a brief test, late at night in bed, I wound up watching the entire film. It all feels a bit like when I bought my first decent set of headphones — I never knew what I was missing, but now I want to revisit all my favorites to experience them more deeply.
Not all 3D content is equal. Few live-action movies were truly filmed with twin cameras in recent years. In fake or poorly converted 3D movies, you’ll often see a “billboard” effect where it looks like there are flat layers of people or objects in the background instead of true depth.
But the biggest catch is that 3D movies aren’t easy to just buy and play. Even though 3D films are still coming to theaters, you can’t necessarily stream them or buy a high-quality copy. 4K Blu-ray doesn’t support 3D at all. 3D Blu-rays were the last discs to offer 3D, and as FlatPanelsHD pointed out last year, that means most physical 3D movies are stuck in the past at 1080p, 24fps, without HDR.
Even 3D Blu-rays aren’t necessarily easy to find: I had to nab a copy of Cave of Forgotten Dreams off eBay, and paid a pretty penny to ship a rare-ish copy of Into the Spider-Verse from Thailand.
Here’s the good news: The leading headset makers are starting to convince Hollywood it’s time to stream their 3D collections instead.
In 2024, the Apple Vision Pro launched with by far the best 3D movie experience yet, now with 4K, HDR, spatial audio, some (Avatar) films at 48fps, HEVC encoding, free 3D upgrades for many films you’d already purchased in 2D, and exclusive access to the largest catalog of 3D films in existence on Disney Plus. (Modern Disney animated films are natively rendered in digital 3D, and most Disney-owned Marvel films got a 3D conversion to jazz up their theatrical appeal.)
Soon, you’ll no longer need a $3,500 Apple headset to watch those films or convert them from old discs — you’ll be able to stream them with a $350 Meta Quest 3S or $600 Quest 3, as well as the new $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, Meta director of entertainment Sarah Malkin confirms to The Verge.
Meta’s headset will offer 3D movies to subscribers in the Disney Plus, HBO, Paramount Plus, and Peacock apps, she says, with some of that starting later this fall.
And by the time the Meta VR Glasses launch in spring, there will be “hundreds of 3D films available” to rent or buy though Meta’s TV app, as well as some free 3D content. They shouldn’t cost more than traditional movies, either, she says: “Our 3D movies will also be in line with typical pricing for 2D Ultra High Definition (UHD) films.”
(In case you’re wondering, she also says the Meta VR Glasses’ three-hour battery life quote should cover a full 3D movie “watched in Theater mode if starting with the device fully charged.”)
In the meanwhile, I’m experiencing 3D the hacky way: by ripping discs. Every time I walk into a thrift store, I hunt for a 3D Blu-ray or two. I pop them into an old external USB Blu-ray reader, then let MakeMKV spend half an hour per movie to produce a 30-to-40GB multi-view (MVC) file. I pop that into BD3D2MK3D for another 50 minutes per movie to spit out a high-quality 3840 x 1080 “Full-SBS” file that’s half the size of the MVC.
I drop that onto an SD card, pop it into the Steam Deck, plug in the Xreal glasses, fire up VLC Media Player, then flip the glasses into 3D mode. It’s a lot of friction, but for me, the payoff is worth it.
Even though I’m mostly watching old movies, it feels like a taste of the future. But you know what they say: Everything old is eventually new again.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : l'astuce inédite d'Apple pour rendre la pliure de l'écran invisible sur le long terme
articles.text:
La sortie de l’iPhone Duo mi-octobre approche à grands pas et chaque jour apporte son lot de nouvelles concernant le premier smartphone pliant d’Apple.
L’un des principaux axes de communication de la marque à la pomme pour cette nouvelle catégorie de produits repose évidemment sur l’écran pliant et sa pliure, présentée comme invisible.
La pliure apparente : un problème de physique
Il conviendra de le vérifier lors du test du produit chez 01net, mais, même si Apple est parvenu à réaliser cet exploit, l’expérience accumulée par ses concurrents démontre qu’à terme, même les pliures les plus invisibles finissent par apparaître. Le fait de plier et déplier sans cesse le smartphone finit par réduire cet avantage chez toutes les marques, jusqu’à parfois atteindre le stade ultime : une pliure visible en permanence, même lorsque l’écran est bien lumineux et placé en face de vous.
Cela s’explique facilement : pour obtenir un écran pliant, les constructeurs ne peuvent pas recourir au verre, trop rigide. Ils ont donc mis au point diverses couches appliquées sur la dalle OLED afin d’imiter les écrans traditionnels et leur robustesse, tout en masquant la pliure.
Une solution simple : proposer un filtre de remplacement
C’est là que réside la solution d’Apple pour maintenir une pliure invisible : pouvoir changer la couche supérieure. La démarche paraît plutôt maligne, puisque c’est elle qui accumule les traces d’usure, les micro-rayures, mais aussi les marques les plus visibles causées par des milliers de pliages et dépliages.
Dans une interview accordée au compte TikTok @angietutorials, Kate Bergeron, vice-présidente en charge de l’ingénierie matérielle, a livré cette information :
 « Le revêtement mat de l’écran est très efficace pour, disons, atténuer les traces de pliure. Mais il y a une couche de protection par-dessus, et nous avons mené un travail d’ingénierie considérable pour que celle-ci s’use le plus lentement possible et pour vous permettre de profiter au maximum des performances de cette couche. Elle est d’ailleurs remplaçable, ce qui est un véritable atout pour le client : vous pouvez retirer cette couche et en installer une nouvelle. »
On notera dans cette déclaration qu’Apple a semble-t-il tenté de jouer sur les deux tableaux : concevoir une couche supérieure qui tienne le plus longtemps possible, tout en offrant la possibilité de la remplacer.
Nous avons même une idée de ce que cela pourrait coûter, du moins pour les abonnés au service d’assurance de la marque, AppleCare. Un utilisateur de X (Twitter) a repéré que le remplacement coûterait 19 dollars en magasin. Impossible de connaître le montant en euros à ce stade, ni le prix d’une intervention hors AppleCare.

articles.title: La Commission européenne veut se passer de Microsoft Teams, mais son alternative est très critiquée
articles.text:
La Commission européenne teste Element Pro pour réduire sa dépendance à Microsoft et disposer d’une solution de secours à Teams. Mais entre ambitions souveraines et usages quotidiens, les premiers retours ne sont pas franchement enthousiastes.
La Commission européenne veut pouvoir continuer à communiquer même si Microsoft Teams devenait indisponible. Depuis cet été, elle teste Element Pro, une plateforme collaborative qu’elle héberge sur ses propres infrastructures et qu’elle présente comme un « back-up souverain » à l’outil de Microsoft. Un choix qui s’inscrit dans la volonté de Bruxelles de mieux contrôler ses systèmes et ses données, mais suscite déjà de vives critiques en interne selon POLITICO.
Un plan B fondé sur des technologies ouvertes
Dans le détail, Element Pro se présente comme une plateforme collaborative intégrant une messagerie pour les conversations individuelles et de groupe, un système de partage de fichiers, des salles de travail, ainsi que la prise en charge des appels audio et vidéo. Des fonctions très proches de celles de Teams, mais déployées selon un modèle très différent : la Commission héberge directement la plateforme sur ses propres infrastructures, quand le service de Microsoft dépend de l’environnement cloud de l’entreprise américaine.
Element Pro s’appuie sur Matrix, un standard ouvert de communication qui permet à une administration ou à une grande organisation d’exploiter et d’administrer elle-même sa plateforme. Bruxelles conserve de cette manière un contrôle beaucoup plus direct sur l’infrastructure du service et sur les données qu’elle héberge, tout en réduisant sa dépendance à Microsoft. Le choix d’un standard ouvert limite aussi l’enfermement dans l’écosystème d’un seul éditeur, puisque le protocole sur lequel reposent les communications n’appartient pas à Element, même si l’entreprise reste l’un de ses principaux contributeurs et conserve ses propres composants professionnels.
Cette technologie a d’ailleurs déjà trouvé sa place dans plusieurs administrations européennes. En France, elle sert de base à Tchap, la messagerie sécurisée des agents de l’État, tandis que la DINUM a rejoint en 2025 la Matrix.org Foundation afin de contribuer plus directement à l’évolution du standard.
L’Allemagne s’appuie elle aussi sur Matrix pour plusieurs services publics, dont BundesMessenger, la Suède l’utilise dans SAFOS, sa suite collaborative souveraine, et le Luxembourg dans LuxChat4Gov, sa messagerie destinée aux agents publics. Aux Pays-Bas, Matrix est intégré à MijnBureau, un environnement de travail souverain encore en phase pilote, tandis qu’il sert de base à BEAM, la messagerie gouvernementale belge.
Une alternative qui ne fait pas l'unanimité
Un projet qui ne manque donc pas d’arguments, mais peine visiblement à convaincre dans les bureaux de la Commission. Des échanges internes font état de critiques particulièrement sévères de la part de plusieurs fonctionnaires européens, qui s’interrogent aussi bien sur l’intérêt du nouvel outil que sur sa capacité à remplacer efficacement Teams en cas de besoin.
Dans ces échanges, l’un dit ne pas comprendre la valeur ajoutée d’Element Pro, tandis qu’un autre résume son expérience en deux mots : « absolute shit ». Un troisième estime qu’en cas de rupture avec les technologies américaines, les États-Unis « gagneraient instantanément » si Element Pro devait prendre le relais de Teams.
Bref, un lot de critiques plutôt vives, auquel Matthew Hodgson, patron d’Element, répond en rappelant que la Commission européenne se trouve encore en phase de test. À ces problèmes de jeunesse s’ajoute aussi la difficulté, très classique, de remplacer un outil ancré depuis des années dans les habitudes de travail par une interface dont les agents doivent encore apprivoiser la logique de navigation, l’organisation et les automatismes.

articles.title: Minecraft dans GTA, Call of Duty dans Skyrim… les jeux commencent à fusionner dans tous les sens à cause des agents IA
articles.text:
Les moddeurs PC mélangent les univers des jeux vidéo depuis bien longtemps. Créer ces fusions improbables demande généralement beaucoup de code, de nombreux essais et pas mal de temps. Mais depuis ce mardi 29 septembre, les démonstrations se succèdent sur les réseaux sociaux, et semblent demander bien moins d’efforts.
On peut construire avec les blocs de Minecraft dans Los Santos et faire exploser les voitures de GTA 5 avec de la TNT. Les armes et les zombies de Call of Duty: Black Ops apparaissent aussi dans Skyrim. JV a récemment consacré une vidéo à cette tendance, avec des rencontres improbables entre des jeux qui n’ont pas été conçus pour fonctionner ensemble.
Ces créations viennent de projets différents, et leurs auteurs ne disent pas tous s’ils ont utilisé l’IA. Certaines montrent toutefois le travail que l’on peut désormais confier aux assistants de programmation pour créer des mods.
Ce que les agents IA changent pour les moddeurs
Faire interagir deux jeux demande de comprendre comment chacun fonctionne, puis d’écrire le code qui les relie. Où se trouve le joueur ? Comment déplacer la caméra ? Comment déclencher une explosion au bon endroit ? Chaque jeu possède ses propres façons de gérer ces actions, que le créateur doit parvenir à faire communiquer.
Les assistants de programmation comme Claude Code, Codex ou Cursor peuvent prendre en charge une partie de ce travail. Ils disposent d’outils pour examiner des fichiers, écrire du code, lancer des programmes et vérifier le résultat par eux-mêmes. Le créateur peut donc leur confier une bonne partie du travail, puis les orienter au fil des essais et des problèmes rencontrés.
Les entreprises de l’IA misent déjà beaucoup sur ces agents pour de nombreux usages. Le modding en profite à son tour.
Dans Minecraft × GTA, deux jeux tournent en même temps
Rehan Sheikh, à l’origine du mélange Minecraft et GTA 5, a rassemblé ses méthodes dans Universal Modder. Ce projet fournit aux agents des instructions, des outils (plugins et skills) et une documentation sur les jeux déjà explorés. Il leur permet de retrouver les solutions existantes et de réutiliser celles découvertes lors des précédents projets. Les outils des communautés de modding restent essentiels : l’agent s’appuie sur eux pour construire la modification demandée.
Le mélange de Minecraft et GTA 5 fait tourner les deux jeux en même temps sur un seul PC. Un mod dans chacun d’eux leur permet de communiquer. GTA transmet à Minecraft la position et la caméra du joueur, tandis que les images des deux jeux sont réunies pour donner l’impression de parcourir un seul monde.
Le programme tient aussi compte de la distance des objets : un lampadaire de GTA peut cacher une partie d’une maison en blocs, qui masque elle-même une voiture située derrière. Les constructions deviennent également des obstacles pour les véhicules.
Enfin, les mods traduisent certaines actions d’un jeu dans l’autre. Une explosion de TNT dans Minecraft déclenche une explosion dans GTA. Les PNJ de GTA qui se trouvent à côté réagissent comme à n’importe quelle explosion du jeu. Les deux jeux conservent donc leurs règles, avec une liaison qui permet de faire interagir certains de leurs éléments.
L’ère de l’IA dans le modding, une vraie tendance
Avec l’IA, ces croisements d’univers improbables se montent désormais en quelques jours, là où il fallait jusqu’ici bien plus de temps. Des projets que beaucoup n’auraient jamais lancés en temps normal voient ainsi le jour. Le modding suit le même chemin que d’autres domaines : on décrit ce que l’on veut obtenir, et l’IA prend en charge une partie du travail technique.
La vague semble être partie de la fusion de Minecraft et d’Elden Ring publiée par Tobyn Jacobs, que la documentation d’Universal Modder mentionne d’ailleurs. Ce mod reste une démonstration. Son auteur n’a donné ni lien de téléchargement ni date de sortie, et ses premiers messages ne disent pas quel outil d’IA il a utilisé.
Depuis, d’autres moddeurs s’y sont mis. Le youtubeur Chasm montre bien cet enthousiasme dans une vidéo consacrée à SkyCraft, son mélange de Minecraft et de Skyrim. On y retrouve les blocs, l’inventaire et les armes du premier dans le monde du second.
Les titres de ses vidéos donnent le ton : « La nouvelle génération du modding », mais aussi « Est-ce le futur du jeu vidéo ? ». Chasm invite même ses spectateurs à rejoindre son serveur Discord pour trouver d’autres mélanges improbables à faire.
Ces joueurs reprennent ainsi la main sur des jeux qu’ils possèdent, sans attendre qu’un éditeur leur propose ce genre de croisement.
Cette liberté de création se heurte toutefois au droit d’auteur : posséder un jeu n’autorise pas à redistribuer son contenu, même gratuitement. Utiliser les fichiers déjà installés chez le joueur évite de les partager, sans garantir la légalité du mod. Les agents IA ouvrent de nouvelles possibilités, mais ne donnent pas davantage de droits sur les jeux qu’ils permettent de transformer.
Ces mods demandent malgré tout du temps et une supervision humaine. Rehan Sheikh indique avoir eu besoin d’environ deux jours de sessions avec Claude Code pour Minecraft × GTA. Un humain dirigeait le travail et se chargeait des clics que le projet réserve aux humains.
